### Student Build Pipeline: T4 — the reviewed plan is the plan that ships (2026-08-10)
- [x] **Closed the defect where dry-run and commit each regenerated, so a reviewed plan was not the plan persisted**
  - Date: 2026-08-10
  - Session: CC-20260809-b7k2
  - What changed: `backend/src/services/sbp/planHash.ts` (PURE) and `planStore.ts` (I/O). The pilot's dry-run and commit each called the model independently — which is exactly how a plan reviewed at 6/3/1/1/1 was persisted as 8/1/1/1/1, with different requirement numbering. Now the plan is written **once** at generation as a `draft` in `build_plans`, review reads that row, and `publishPlan` **promotes the same row** — there is no INSERT on the publish path at all. `publishPlan` optionally takes the SHA the reviewer was shown and refuses with `HashMismatch` if the stored row has changed underneath them, which turns "the reviewed plan is the published plan" from an intention into an enforced invariant. Hashing is canonical (keys sorted recursively before serialization) so a structurally identical plan built in a different key order does not hash differently and get rejected as tampered. Publish is idempotent, and promoting a version supersedes any previously published one. `saveIntake` stores the wizard answers verbatim, idempotent on `project_id` so a retry after a failed generation reuses the same intake rather than stacking rows. Raw SQL with results typed at the call site — `build_plans`/`build_intake` have no Sequelize model, which `backend/CLAUDE.md` explicitly permits on that condition.
  - Verification: **98/98 tests pass** across six suites (`JEST_EXIT=0`), up from 80. The invariant is tested directly rather than asserted: the publish test checks the promoted plan hashes identically to the reviewed one **and** scans every issued query to prove no `INSERT INTO build_plans` occurred on that path — a regeneration would fail the test. A tampering test swaps the stored plan and confirms publish raises `HashMismatch` instead of shipping it. Hash tests cover stability, key-order independence, content sensitivity, and specifically that **moving a story between releases changes the hash** — the exact skew that went undetected in the pilot. Version selection is asserted to happen inside the INSERT (`COALESCE(MAX(version),0)+1`) so two concurrent generations cannot claim the same version, with the unique index as backstop. Intake tests cover ON CONFLICT idempotency, a 4,000-char idea stored verbatim, and that absent fields default to NULL rather than being invented.
  - Notes: 6 of 17 tasks. Nothing deployed, nothing merged to main. Next is T5 (pure document renderers), which is the last piece before the GitHub write path.

- [x] Deploy log: Week 1 video walkthroughs live on production — plus a prod stash-pop incident, caught and fully recovered
  - Date: 2026-08-10
  - Session: CC-20260806-b4k2
  - What changed: deployed the Part 0 / Part 3 video walkthroughs (#1338) to production. **Incident during the deploy, disclosed in full:** the deploy script paired `git stash push -q -- scripts/cron-env-wrapper.sh` with a later `git stash pop`. That pairing is unsafe on this VPS. `git stash push -- <path>` creates **no stash entry at all** when the path is already clean, and by this run the cron hotfix had been committed upstream — so the push was a no-op and the following `pop` popped **`stash@{0}`, which belonged to a different session** (`pre-deploy CC-20260730-h4q9`). That dumped ~513 modified files and 100 conflicted paths into the prod working tree and failed the backend build (`BUILD_EXIT=1`), leaving the previously-deployed image running. **Nothing was lost:** because the pop hit conflicts, git retained the stash entry, verified still present as `stash@{0}` with all 47 stashes intact. Recovered by inspecting first (`git stash list`, conflict count, hotfix state) rather than reflexively re-running: confirmed the cron hotfix now lives in HEAD (so it never needed stashing), confirmed the other session's stash was retained, then `git reset --hard HEAD` to drop the popped content — which does not touch stashes. Verified 0 conflicts, 0 modified tracked files, `HEAD == origin/main`, hotfix present, 47 stashes still listed. Checked the 38 surviving untracked files for build risk before rebuilding (`0` untracked `.ts`/`.tsx` under `backend/src` or `frontend/src`) and deliberately did NOT `git clean` them — they are pre-existing prod-local artifacts and some may belong to another session.
  - Verification: backend rebuilt `BUILD_EXIT=0`, health confirmed via `docker exec ... node -e fetch` (the image has no wget) after ~15s. Seeder applied then re-run: `applied` → `already-current`, proving the jsonb key-order idempotency fix holds in production. Live DB read-back of card `5653f10c`: **12,360 chars** (was 9,975), **7 sections**, **11 links**, **7 YouTube links** — read out of Postgres, not inferred from the deploy log. Earlier in the session the same read-back confirmed the workshop card (6 stages / 8 prompts, retitled) and the Claude Code 101 card, and confirmed the served bundle `main.53927f98.js` contains `allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox` so the authored links actually open.
  - Notes: **Root lesson, worth carrying:** never pair a blind `git stash push -- <path>` with `git stash pop` on this VPS. Prod carries 47 stashes from many sessions, so a no-op push followed by a pop silently reaches into someone else's work. Use `git stash list` count before/after, or address the specific stash by ref, or — better — do not stash at all once the local change is committed upstream. The safe recovery shape when it does happen: inspect before acting, confirm the stash entry survived, then `git reset --hard` (stashes are untouched by reset), and never `git clean` a shared prod tree.

### Sponsor magic-link: fix a 500-on-junk-token crash, add an audit trail, and repair the blank dashboard (2026-08-10)
- [x] **Two live-only defects on the public sponsor surface, plus durable auditing for magic-link issue and access**
  - Date: 2026-08-10

(1) **`GET /api/sponsor/verify` returned 500 for an empty or non-UUID `?token=`, and wrote no audit record.** `sponsors.portal_token` is a `DataTypes.UUID` column, so Postgres raises a type error on a malformed literal instead of simply not matching, and the throw happened inside `Sponsor.findOne` before anything could be logged — so probing the endpoint with junk produced server errors and left no trace. A valid-shaped but unknown UUID behaved correctly; only malformed input was affected. Now guarded by a UUID shape test at the top of `verifySponsorPortalToken`: anything not UUID-shaped is a bad link, gets the same 401 as any other, and records `link_rejected` with reason `malformed_token`. (2) **New `sponsor_portal_audit_log`** (`SponsorPortalAuditLog` model + `sponsorAuditService`) recording `link_generated` on issue — written before the send, so a link that is minted but never delivered is still on record — and `link_accessed` / `link_rejected` on both outcomes of verify, each with a correlation id, redacted email, client IP and user agent. Tokens are stored as a **SHA-256 fingerprint, never plaintext**, so an access can be joined back to the generation event that issued it without the table becoming a credential store; a value that was never a token is not fingerprinted at all. Audit writes are best-effort — a failed insert logs `sponsor_portal_audit_write_failed` and continues rather than locking a customer out of their dashboard. `ensureSponsorPortalAuditSchema()` added to the boot sequence, since boot runs no global sync and the table would otherwise never exist in prod. Replaced with an explicit `ApiSponsorDashboard` type, a mapper, and a check that validates the fields actually used. Two related defects fixed in passing: the React key was `p.email`, but the endpoint deliberately does not expose participant emails to the sponsor surface, so every live row would have keyed on `undefined` (participants now carry an `id`, `enrollment_id` for live data); and Demo Day membership now reads the server's own `demo_day_candidates` list rather than re-deriving the rule client-side, so the two cannot drift.

### Student Build Pipeline: five dead gate rules, and a repair loop that made plans worse (2026-08-10)
- [x] **Three builds fired at production simultaneously; one failed the gate and ended with more violations than it started with**
  - Date: 2026-08-10
  - Session: CC-20260809-b7k2
  - What changed: The concurrency test Ali asked for (3 parallel builds, real test enrollments, `SBP_PROVISION_CONCURRENCY=3`) passed 2 of 3 and exposed two defects behind the third. **(1) Five of the seven `UNFALSIFIABLE` regexes in `planGate.ts` could never match, and neither could the `LAYER_TITLE` backstop.** The file was originally written through a shell heredoc that interpreted `\b`, leaving a literal **0x08 backspace byte** in the source — so `/\bhigh[- ]quality\b/i` was really `/<0x08>high[- ]quality<0x08>/i`, a pattern demanding a control character. `\w` survived (no shell escape for it), which is why the corruption looked selective and plausible; it rendered as correct source in every editor, diff, and review. Only `relevant regulations` and `user[- ]friendly` (the two with no `\b`) ever fired. All 13 bytes replaced; a repo-wide scan found none elsewhere. **(2) The repair loop could not fix requirement-level violations and was not monotone.** It returned only stories, so `requirement_unfalsifiable` on REQ-008 ("a user-friendly interface") was structurally unfixable — no story that can ever be written repairs a vague requirement, so all three attempts burned on a violation it had no vocabulary to address. Worse, asked to fix it, the model bolted on STORY-015 and STORY-016, both near-duplicates of the existing STORY-012, and the three then mutually tripped `story_redundant_scaffold`: the plan went from 3 violations to 6. `planRepair.ts` now (a) accepts corrected **requirements**, merged in place by id — and refuses invented ones, since a repair that adds requirements moves the goalposts it is graded against; (b) accepts `remove_story_ids`, because a subsuming story is only fixable by deletion or narrowing and add/replace left the model no move but the one that caused the violation; (c) **discards any attempt that does not strictly reduce the violation count**, keeping the previous plan, so repair can never hand back something worse than it received; (d) carries a per-rule remedy table into the prompt, since without it the model's only instinct is "add a story".
  - Verification: 231/231 backend SBP tests green across 12 suites, up from 205 — including a new `planRepair.test.ts` (11 cases, none previously existed for that module) whose fixtures reproduce the exact production failure, and `planGateRegexes.test.ts`, which asserts every pattern matches the phrase it was written for **through `gatePlan` rather than in isolation** (a hand-typed copy of the regex is correct, so an isolation test would have stayed green against the corrupted constant) plus a source-level scan for 0x08/0x0b/0x0c/0x07/0x00. Scoped `tsc --noEmit` clean on both changed modules. Concurrency evidence, on prod: 3 builds accepted `HTTP 202` simultaneously, 2 reached `drafted` in 25s and 30s, both gate-clean, both balanced (3/2/1/2/2 and 3/2/2/1/2 against a ceiling of 4.0), both published to 5 lists / 10 tasks each with 10/10 prompts over 1200 chars, and the two plans were distinct — no cross-contamination under load.
  - Notes: **Fixing the regexes makes the gate strictly stricter**, so the pass rate has to be re-measured on production before class rather than assumed — the repair loop can now fix the `requirement_unfalsifiable` class in place, which is the one the newly-live patterns will surface most. Two broader lessons. A regex constant with no test asserting it *matches* something is indistinguishable from a comment: 27 existing gate tests were green the whole time because not one exercised those five phrases. And a repair loop needs the same monotonicity guarantee as any optimiser — this one was free to degrade its input, and did. This is the fifth defect in this workstream invisible to the test suite and visible only in real output.

- [x] **The gate contradicted itself, and the student paid for it: blocking vs advisory violations**
  - Date: 2026-08-10
  - Session: CC-20260809-b7k2
  - What changed: Re-running the 3-way concurrency test after deploying the repair fix took the failing build from **6 violations to 1** — repair rewrote REQ-008 in place ("The system should provide a user-friendly interface" became "Every screen the director uses must complete its primary action in three clicks or fewer"), and the layer stories were gone. The one that survived was `story_redundant_scaffold` on STORY-010, *"Ensure idempotent notification and logging"*, for subsuming STORY-003 and STORY-009. **That story is the r0 trust spine** — the thing `r0_no_trust_spine` explicitly demands, and which by its nature cites the notification requirement AND the audit requirement that other stories own. Two gate rules in direct conflict, and the cost of the standoff was a student seeing an empty Projects page. Split `GateRule` into **9 blocking** and **8 advisory**. Blocking means *the plan would mislead the student about what they are building, or write broken data*: `must_uncovered` (claims a requirement nothing delivers), `dangling_*`/`malformed_*` (materialization writes rows the portal cannot render — a `blocked_by` pointing at no story locks a task forever), `r0_missing`/`r0_not_ungated` (no first release, or every r0 story blocked, which locks the student out of starting at all), `invented_vendor` (tells them to integrate Stripe when their brief said PaySimple). Everything else is a quality warning that rides along with the plan. `gate.ok` still means spotless and repair still tries to clear everything; what changed is only what happens **when repair runs out of attempts**. `publishBuild` now refuses on blocking violations alone and names them in the 409 rather than saying "unresolved gate violations", and the Projects page reports the real cause instead of asserting "N requirement(s) are not yet covered by a story" for every failure regardless of what actually went wrong. Also widened the `story_redundant_scaffold` repair remedy: it pointed the model at the subsuming story, when the genuine duplicate is often a **subsumed** one (here STORY-003 "Notify director of upcoming deadlines" duplicated STORY-001, which already covered REQ-004).
  - Verification: 257/257 SBP tests green across 13 suites, up from 231. New `planGateSeverity.test.ts` pins the blocking list as a literal — moving a rule across that line changes whether students see broken plans, so it must be a deliberate edit to the test — and the load-bearing cases are the **negative** ones: a blocking violation among four advisory ones still blocks; a plan with an uncovered must-have is never publishable however tidy; a plan whose r0 is fully blocked is never publishable. Four new orchestrator tests cover refuse-on-blocking, publish-on-advisory-only, refuse-on-mixed, and that the 409 names the offending requirement. Reconstructed the exact production plan (project 2c9953ce) as a fixture and asserted it now publishes. Backend and frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean.
  - Notes: **This is a deliberate loosening and Ali should weigh in.** Before it, `published` meant "spotless"; now it means every must-have is covered, every reference resolves, and r0 is startable — the invariant that actually protects the student — while style problems are surfaced rather than fatal. I made the call because the alternative in a live cohort is that roughly one student in three completes the wizard and gets nothing, which fails the stated goal ("all students will have their story's and releases created") worse than a plan with one redundant story in it. **What is not built:** the advisory warnings are stored on the plan but nothing renders them yet, so a student currently cannot see that their plan has a known rough edge — that UI is the obvious next piece. The underlying rule conflict is also still there: `r0_no_trust_spine` and `story_redundant_scaffold` will keep disagreeing about the trust-spine story, and the honest fix is to teach the scaffold rule that r0's trust spine is legitimately cross-cutting rather than to keep asking repair to work around it.

Sent live to ali@colaberry.com before scheduling: `accepted: ["ali@colaberry.com"], rejected: []`, Mandrill id `93b4c47f-04e4-ba32-b09d-d89cc76dad8c`, body 92.7 KB plus the 821 KB dashboard attached. Idempotency verified by re-running the real send: refused with "already sent", no second message. Layout verified in headless Chromium at inbox width across four slices, not just by reading markup; emitted HTML has 84/84 tables and 326/326 cells balanced and zero external asset references.
  - Notes: **The schedule gate lives in the script, not in cron, on purpose.** The VPS runs UTC and no crontab line sets `CRON_TZ`, so a fixed UTC time would drift an hour at each DST change and deliver the briefing *after* the meeting for half the year. Setting `CRON_TZ` in the shared crontab is worse: in vixie cron it applies to every line after it and would silently re-time unrelated jobs. So cron fires `45 13,14,15 * * 1,2` and the script reads the Central wall clock from the zone database and decides. Tests assert that across **both** CST and CDT exactly one of those three ticks fires, and that it is the right one. A send failure raises a distinct-subject alert email (`[FAILED] Intern Delivery briefing...`) rather than dying quietly in a log, since a silent cron is the documented failure mode of the existing reporting suite. - [x] **PaySimple webhook: fix the signature check that was rejecting 100% of real deliveries (uppercase vs lowercase hex)**
  - Date: 2026-08-12
  - Session: CC-20260812-k4rp
  - What changed: Investigating why Arinze Ohagwu's payment never linked (see the entry above) turned up a live outage: **every** PaySimple webhook was being rejected `400` with `[Webhook] PaySimple signature verification failed` — 11 deliveries between 17:12 and 18:51 UTC on 2026-08-12, all from PaySimple's `54.186.163.123`, zero successes. Ruled out the obvious causes with evidence: the signature header IS present (0 "no signature header" warnings), the secret IS configured (64 chars, and hashing the value across 5 `.env` backups to 2026-07-21 proved it **unchanged** — the 2026-08-10 21:56 `.env` edit only added `GITHUB_TOKEN` and two `SBP_*` keys). PaySimple exposes no webhook-config API (probed 11 candidate routes, all 404 / "route does not exist"), so I captured a real delivery off the internal docker bridge with `tcpdump` (read-only, no deploy) and tested it. **The digest was byte-identical to ours apart from letter case:** PaySimple sends `5F0738DD23FE...` while Node's `digest('hex')` returns `5f0738dd23fe...`, and `verifyWebhookSignature` compared the digest TEXT via `timingSafeEqual` (`'5F'` = 0x35,0x46 vs `'5f'` = 0x35,0x66), so it could never match. Fixed by comparing the raw 32 digest BYTES instead of the hex string, decoding the header as hex (either case) or base64 via a new `decodeDigest()` that returns null on a malformed header rather than comparing a truncated buffer. This is the **third** distinct cause of "every PaySimple webhook is rejected", after the `JSON.stringify(req.body)` raw-body bug (2026-07-30) and the `express.raw` Content-Type matcher (2026-07-31), which is why the fix is now encoding-agnostic rather than matching one more exact format.
  - Verification: proven against the real captured delivery before writing any code — 445-byte body, received `5F0738DD23FE5E19D28E1722F44FF6E8A6CD8CB39B18DD58450AF2B4ED75D233`, our HMAC over the same bytes with the configured secret `5f0738dd23fe5e19d28e1722f44ff6e8a6cd8cb39b18dd58450af2b4ed75d233`: exact-byte match **false**, case-insensitive match **true**, base64 match **false**. So the secret and the raw-body handling were already correct and case was the entire defect. 6 new unit tests; the load-bearing one asserts the UPPERCASE digest verifies, and it **fails against the unfixed code** (baseline run of the new tests against the old service: 4 failed / 18 passed; with the fix: 1 failed / 21 passed, the 1 being a pre-existing unrelated `findCustomerByEmail` fixture failure). Negative cases kept: right-length-but-not-hex, too-short, empty, wrong payload, and wrong secret all still reject. Full backend jest with normalized comparison of the failing-suite sets: **28 failing suites both with and without the change, zero regressions, zero newly-passing** (an intermediate run showed 29 — a timing-sensitive suite, not this change). `tsc --noEmit`: 15 errors with and without, none in `paysimpleService.ts`.
  - Notes: **The existing test suite is exactly why this shipped.** `verifies valid HMAC signature` built its fixture with `digest('hex')`, i.e. lowercase, so it exercised a format PaySimple never sends and passed against broken code. A test that generates its own input in the wrong format proves nothing about the real integration; the new uppercase test is the one that would have caught it. **Not fixed here:** why Valentine Obiora (08-03) and ammar albazzaz (08-04) were missed — successful webhook activations sit on either side of them, so those look like individual missed deliveries rather than this total failure, and the container logs for those dates were lost to a redeploy before the investigation. **Also worth flagging:** PaySimple retries hard. The delivery I captured was an event first created **2026-08-01**, still being retried 11 days later, so once this is deployed the backlog should drain on its own; the reconciler is idempotent and `usedPids` prevents any double-link if both paths fire. Separately confirmed while investigating: across **all 16** payments the app has ever linked, **0** landed on the customer id we stored at checkout, so the reconciler's customer-id match path has never once worked in production — which makes the checkout-window path in the companion PR the only mechanism currently capable of linking a payment.

Confirmed and root-caused, then found two more with the same signature. **The defect:** PaySimple's *hosted* payment page mints its **own** customer record for the payer, so the charge's `CustomerId` is not the one our app pre-created at checkout — Arinze's checkout created customer `43728423`, his settled $199 (payment `155621427`) landed on `43728431`, minted by the hosted page 4 minutes later. Activation normally comes from the webhook matching `order_external_id` → `subscriptions.payment_ref`, which works (13 subscriptions activated fine); when a delivery is missed, `appPaymentReconcileService` is the safety net — and it could never heal these, for two reasons. (1) It drew candidates from `enrollments.paysimple_customer_id`, but `startCheckout` wrote the customer id **only onto the subscription row**, so 62 of 86 pending checkouts were invisible to it (the candidate query saw **8** rows where the corrected one sees **31**). (2) Even reading the subscription's id would not have matched, because the charge carries the hosted page's customer, not ours. Fixes: `startCheckout` now reuses a customer id we already stored (enrollment, then prior subscription) before minting a new one — `findCustomerByEmail` can only ever return null because PaySimple ignores its own `?email=` filter (probed live: **200 rows returned, 0 with a matching email**), which had turned `findOrCreateCustomer` into create-every-time and gave Arinze's four attempts four duplicate customers — and mirrors that id onto the enrollment (best-effort; the payment link is already valid, so bookkeeping must never fail a live checkout). `reconcileAppPayments` gains a second match path, `matchesAppCheckout`, for the hosted-customer case.
  - Verification: `tsc --noEmit` — **15 errors with the change, 15 on an unmodified `origin/main` baseline, none in either changed file** (the 15 are pre-existing: `axios`/`playwright` are imported but absent from `package.json`). Full backend jest: **28 failed suites / 41 failed tests both with and without the change** (same pre-existing missing-module failures), **7253 passing with vs 7239 baseline — +14, exactly the tests added**, 0 regressions. New scope-guard tests assert the safety-critical negatives: a same-amount charge from a different payer, an amount we never asked for (bootcamp $250), a charge outside the window, and a person with no app-originated checkout are all **rejected**. New checkout tests cover customer reuse, the enrollment mirror, and that checkout still returns `ok` when the mirror write throws. The corrected candidate SQL was executed read-only against the live prod schema before shipping (31 candidates / 24 with pending checkouts). Data heal ran on prod through the normal `activateByRef` path: all 3 now `paid` / `standard` / `member`, routed into "Cohort - July 2026", subscriptions `active` with payment ids linked and billing anchored to the real payment date (Arinze 2026-08-11 → 2026-09-11); his 3 duplicate checkouts canceled. A re-run of the detection sweep afterwards returned **0 remaining, $0.00**.
  - Notes: **Scope doctrine preserved and deliberately reasoned about.** Revenue counts only app-originated payments, and the standing rule forbids matching PaySimple charges by amount/email — that rule exists because an earlier amount-matching ledger over-counted $6,664 against a true $3,038. The new path B does **not** relax it: the thing that brings a payment into scope is still **our own pending subscription row** (our app recorded that it started that checkout, for that exact amount, minutes earlier); the payer email only decides *which* of our pending checkouts a charge belongs to, and never qualifies a payment on its own. Both the file header and the tests state this explicitly so it is not misread later as a regression to email matching. **Revenue impact:** the dashboard was understating by **$398** — Arinze ($199, `payment_status` still `pending`) and ammar albazzaz ($199, marked paid but `amount_paid` NULL, which fails the `amount_paid > 0` filter in `revenuePaymentsService`); Valentine Obiora's $199 was already counted and only needed the payment id linked. **Only Arinze suffered real customer harm** — he paid on 08/10 and was still an Explorer being prompted to subscribe two days later, which is why he retried checkout three times. He was charged exactly **once**; there is no double-billing to refund. **What is not fixed:** the missed webhook deliveries themselves. Container logs for 08/10-08/11 were lost to a redeploy before this investigation, so the cause of the missed callbacks is unproven — the reconciler now heals them within 20 minutes either way, but if the miss rate is climbing, that is a separate investigation and this change would mask it. Worth adding a metric on `linkedByCheckoutWindow`, which is now counted separately in the summary precisely so a rising number is visible.

  - Notes: The original code did `const [, affected] = result; typeof affected === 'number' ? affected : 0`. For Postgres, `sequelize.query()` resolves to `[results, pgResultObject]`, so that always evaluated to 0. **Not merely cosmetic** — the batch loop terminates on `rows === 0`, so it stopped after ONE batch while still reporting `outcome:'complete'`. The first production run had 65 attributable rows, under a single 5000-row batch, so it completed correctly by luck and the DB confirmed 65/65 attributed with 0 remaining. With more than `batchSize` rows it would have silently left the remainder unattributed and claimed success. **The 11 original tests all passed because the mock resolved `[[], rows]` — a shape this dialect never returns — so the suite asserted my assumption about the driver rather than the driver's behaviour.** Found only by running against the real database and noticing that `candidates:65 -> updated:0 -> remaining:0` cannot all be true.

The rules take `devMode` as an explicit argument rather than reading an ambient global, so prod behavior is a single literal `false`. **Also fixed an accounting bug this work exposed:** `guardedSendMail` resolves with an empty `messageId` rather than throwing when a guard stops a send, so `sendSessionReminder` logged `"sent"` **and wrote `status:'sent'` to `communication_logs`** for a message never handed to the transport — with 55 recipients that is 55 phantom deliveries in the audit trail added hours earlier. Blocked sends now record `status:'blocked'`, a third outcome distinct from `'failed'` (which would imply something went wrong when the block was deliberate), using the same `Boolean(info.messageId)` test the training-welcome sender already established.

- [x] **A gate-clean build plan now reaches the student by itself — closing the hole that left five students on the browser fallback**
  - Date: 2026-08-13
  - Session: CC-20260813-p8w3
  - What changed: **The defect.** `runGeneration` ended at `savePlanDraft` + `status='drafted'` and stopped. Publishing is what materialises STORY-000, the cohort due dates and the 3-4k-character Claude Code prompts into `student_tasks`, and **nothing called it**: `publishBuild` had exactly one caller, `POST /api/portal/sbp/builds/:projectId/publish`, which no screen in the product ever hits (`ProjectsPage` imports only `resolveBackendProjectId`, `startBuild`, `pollBuild`). So every gate-clean plan came to rest in `build_plans.status='draft'`, `student_tasks` stayed empty, `enrollments.active_project_id` was never set, and all five students on 2026-08-12/13 spent the evening looking at the browser's local ten-task template. **The fix, in four parts.** (1) `runGeneration` now ends by calling a new `autoPublish()` in the same queued job when `isPublishable(gate.violations)` — it looks up the workspace repo, publishes, and logs `sbp_autopublished`. It passes the just-written draft's `plan_sha256` as `expectedSha`, so a concurrent generation cannot slip a different plan into the promotion. It **cannot throw**: a publish failure is caught, logged as `sbp_autopublish_failed` with an `error_class` and a `recovery` hint, and leaves the build at `drafted` — deliberately NOT `failed`, because `failed` means "regenerate" and telling a student to regenerate a perfectly good plan burns minutes of model time. Kill switch `SBP_AUTO_PUBLISH=off`, defaulting **on**: a second default-OFF flag in front of this would have shipped the fix and left production in exactly the broken state it exists to end. (2) A blocking-violation plan is unchanged — it still fails closed at `gate_failed` — but the poll endpoint now splits `gate.blocking` from `gate.advisory` server-side. The client was taking the first three of the *whole* `violations` array as "why your build was refused", and that array is mostly advisory quality warnings, so a student blocked on an uncovered must-have was being told about a stylistically redundant story. (3) **The student can now tell which build they are looking at.** New `origin: 'local' | 'pipeline'` on `StudentProject`, stamped at birth by `createProjectFromAnswers` and by `backendTreeToProject`, rendered as a chip on the build card and inside the build. The banner explaining a degraded result now renders on **every** Projects view — it previously lived only in the wizard branch, which `handleCreate` leaves on its first line, so it was unmounted before a student could read a word of it. Two of the five never reached the server at all and were told nothing whatsoever. (4) The optimistic placeholder now **claims** its backend project (`pipelineProjectId`, written to localStorage so it survives a reload mid-generation) and `reconcileProjects` supersedes it in place when the real plan lands — guarded on completed work, so a placeholder the student actually ticked something off is kept alongside rather than discarded. Also fixed: `handleCreate`'s post-publish `syncProjectsWithBackend()` was a **no-op**, latched off by the once-per-session guard already tripped on mount, so even a successfully published plan did not appear until a manual reload; new pull-only `refreshProjectsFromBackend()` bypasses the latch. New `services/sbp/workspaceRepo.ts` extracts the repo lookup so the route and the auto path cannot drift.

Backend `src/services/sbp` + `src/routes` together: **28 suites / 447 tests green** (two route suites flaked once under parallel load and passed in isolation and on re-run — a documented pattern in this repo, unrelated to these files). It is a repo-churn problem, not a correctness one — lists, tasks and completion are all genuinely idempotent — and fixing it means fetching and threading the manifest content plus its own tests, so it is logged here rather than smuggled into this change. **Also stale as of this PR:** the local-only `build-student-project` skill (untracked, not on `origin/main`, so unreachable from this worktree) opens with "PUBLISH IS NOT AUTOMATIC" and lists "publish itself", "the localStorage build is never deleted" and "the degradation banner is unreachable after a create" under *prevented only by someone remembering*. Two independent problems, diagnosed from the live database rather than the alert text: the alert engine amplified, and six cron agents were genuinely broken. **`ai_agents.last_error` was a red herring** — four agents carried `out of shared memory`, but Postgres logs showed that as a single nine-error lock burst at 11:00 UTC, never repeated; the field is only written on the throw path, so it had been stale for hours. Ground truth was `ai_agent_activity_logs.details->>'errors'`. **Amplification (the actual "tons of emails"):** `emitAlert` deduped on a one-hour window, so a condition that stays broken minted a fresh alert row and a fresh email every hour forever — 16-23 emails per condition per day. Now deduped on the *condition*: while an alert for the same title+type is unresolved, occurrences fold into it (`occurrence_count`, `last_seen_at` in the existing `metadata` JSONB, no migration) and stay silent, with two escapes so nothing is buried — a severity increase re-notifies immediately, and a condition still firing 24h after the last notification re-notifies once. `campaignWatchdogService` was the single largest source (92/day): it alerted after every auto-rebuild including the ones that re-enrolled 0 leads and created 0 actions, a pure no-op on 4 campaigns every watchdog cycle; it now alerts only when the rebuild changed something and structured-logs the no-op otherwise. **Six agents:** (1) `OpenclawLearningOptimizationAgent` was a *phantom* failure — its work completed fine, then the run-summary INSERT overflowed `ai_agent_activity_logs.action` (varchar(100)) because the orchestrator joins the agent's distinct action names and this agent emits six (137 chars); the throw escaped the orchestrator's success path and recorded the healthy run as FAILED, which is what raised the severity-5 "10/10 runs failed" email Ali screenshotted. Fixed at the single write boundary in `aiEventService.logAgentActivity` so no caller can reintroduce it. (2) `AdmissionsConversationTaskMonitor` ordered by `ChatMessage.created_at`; the model is `timestamps: false` and `chat_messages` names that column `timestamp` — 778 failed runs in 24h. (3) `AdmissionsCallComplianceMonitor` put a SELECT-list alias in a `HAVING` clause, which Postgres does not resolve — `column "call_count" does not exist` every 15 minutes; the aggregate is now repeated via `where(fn('COUNT', col('id')), Op.gt, 1)`. (4)+(5) `AccessControlGuardianAgent` and `CodeSecurityAuditAgent` statically scan TypeScript source, and **the production image ships only compiled `dist`** — their hardcoded `path.resolve(__dirname, '../../../../..')` resolved to `/` in-container, so they looked for `/backend/src` and could never succeed anywhere but a dev checkout. New shared `sourceTreeRoot.ts` walks up for a real `backend/src` (bounded depth, honours `PROJECT_ROOT`) and returns null when there is no source tree; both agents now skip deliberately with a structured log instead of reporting a phantom error. (6) `OpenclawMarketSignalAgent` scans 11 platforms and Reddit persistently 403s this datacenter IP; one blocked source marked all 52 daily runs failed while the other ten scanned fine — per-platform failures are now recorded in actions and structured-logged, and only a total outage (every platform down) is a run failure.

- [x] **Verification latch: fix three ways an already-merged loop let a student's verified work disappear (fixes #1463)**
  - Date: 2026-08-14
  - Session: CC-20260814-r7t3
  - What changed: A fix to code **already merged to main** and undeployed only by timing. Three defects, found by auditing the verification loop from PR #1463 against the rule Ali stated when he ruled that student build repos are student-owned: **evidence lives in our database, the repo is only where verification happens.** All three were one mistake â€” `student_tasks.verified_at` is an immutable latch and `verification_json` is a mutable snapshot of the last repo read, and every display path read the second while ignoring the first, which quietly promoted the repo from evidence into record. (1) A **successful** read with no progress file overwrote `verification_json` for every story unconditionally, so a student who deleted `.colaberry/` and pressed Sync watched six verified stories render as `not_started` while `verified_at` sat untouched in the column underneath. (2) The 100-commit read window downgraded `verified` to `submitted` once an evidence commit scrolled out of it â€” **with no student misbehaviour at all**; falling out of a read window is time passing. (3) `xp_earned` was looked up under a key re-derived from the **current** repo sha while the award row in `evidence_records` is keyed on the sha frozen at award time, so a force-push or squash orphaned a banked award and that story read 0 XP forever, with the row sitting in the table the whole time. Fixed at the cause rather than as three patches. New pure `backend/src/services/sbp/verification/verificationLatch.ts` holds the rule: `applyVerificationLatch(live, latch, prior)` can only ever HOLD a story at verified â€” it never invents one, returns the live record byte-identical when the read agrees, and carries the frozen evidence sha forward while recording what the live read actually said in `live_state` so a degraded repo stays visible rather than hidden. Applied on the **write** (`buildVerificationService`, so the stored blob never states something the record contradicts, and the summary rollup recounts from the latched records rather than the raw verdicts) **and again on the read** (`projectTreeDto.toTaskVerificationDto`, the one function every display surface goes through, so a blob written by an older release, a replay, or a future caller that forgets still cannot show verified work as undone). The actual root fix for (3) is a new column: the evidence sha existed **only inside a log line**, so nothing durable could be joined to it â€” `student_tasks.verified_ref` now persists it under the same first-write-wins discipline as `verified_at`, and `verifiedStoryXp` reads the award through it, gated on the latch rather than on the live verdict, with a story-prefix fallback (`STORY-001@â€¦`, safe because of the `@` delimiter) for any row verified before the column existed. A latched story also carries a sentence that leads with the reassurance â€” "Verified, and it stays verified â€¦ nothing you do to the repo can take it away" â€” instead of the stale "no commit names this story", which reads as an accusation about work that is already done.
  - Verification: **Zero regressions, proven by baseline comparison.** Full backend jest on a clean `origin/main` worktree: 26 failed suites / 33 failed tests / 566 passed suites / 8045 passed tests. On this branch: **25 failed / 32 failed tests / 570 passed suites / 8086 passed tests** â€” no new failing suite, +4 suites and +41 tests passing. (`projectRoutes.test.ts` failed on baseline and passes here; it is a flaky DB-dependent suite, not something this branch fixed.) `tsc --noEmit` clean on both stacks (backend shows only the 2 pre-existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` resolution errors present on baseline). 3 new test files, 41 tests. The three defects are tested as the narrated scenarios they are, not as abstractions: **"A student deletes .colaberry/ and presses Sync"** â€” six stories stay verified, the records WRITTEN BACK say verified with the frozen sha (not just the response), the run awards nothing new, and a build that had verified nothing still shows the honest empty state; **"A story verifies, then 100+ more commits land"** â€” STORY-001 stays verified against a 100-commit window that no longer contains its evidence, while the five stories that genuinely have no commit are still reported honestly as `submitted`; **"A student force-pushes after a story was awarded"** â€” XP still reads 25, the lookup asks for `STORY-001@aaaâ€¦` and never `STORY-001@bbbâ€¦`, and no second award is recorded when the same work re-verifies under a new sha. Plus a pure suite on the latch itself (it never invents a verification; an unlatched story stays exactly where the read put it) and DTO tests proving a verified task whose blob was lost entirely still renders verified while an unverified task with no blob is still null.
  - Notes: **Opened as PR #1465, separate from #1464 (Repo Connect) on purpose** â€” #1464 introduces a step that has never run for a student, while this fixes shipped code, so the connect flow must not hold the safety fix hostage and vice versa. They touch disjoint files and can merge in either order; **this one should go first.** A one-paragraph statement of the rule and of the fact that these three were caught by auditing against it is now in Â§6 of `docs/BUILD_VERIFICATION_CONTRACT.md`, aimed squarely at the next person adding a display surface, because reaching for `verification_json` alone is a reasonable-looking mistake: the blob is right there, it has a `state` field, and it is correct almost all of the time â€” right up until the one moment a student is most likely to panic. Â§9's "commit window" and "revocation" entries were corrected to match the new behaviour rather than left contradicting it. **Still required before this is real:** `ensureSbpSchema` must run against production for the `verified_ref` column (catalog-only ALTER, nullable, no default, no table rewrite â€” but unrun it means Sequelize silently drops the write and every XP lookup takes the prefix fallback), and nothing in the portal renders `task.verification` yet, so the reassuring sentence a latched story now carries has no surface to appear on. **Not deployed, not merged, no email sent.**

That is how `StudentProgressMonitor` sat disabled for **five months** — seeded `enabled=false` by commit `c1f2e4ac` ("Add Governance Command Center", 2026-03-12) on the very day the row was created, `updated_by` NULL so no human ever touched it — while the UI reported it as applied. `aiOpsScheduler.ts` now keeps a live `Map` of every task it creates and exposes `reloadAIOpsSchedules()`, which re-reads the governance DB and reconciles running tasks (start / stop / reschedule / unchanged). Both governance write routes call it and return an `applied: {live, action}` block so a caller can distinguish "saved and live" from "saved only"; a reload failure degrades to `live:false` with a restart-required message rather than failing the request, since the row is already committed. Deliberate: if the DB read throws, reconcile does **nothing** — falling back to hardcoded defaults would silently re-enable jobs an operator had switched off. **(2) The no-sends watchdog cried wolf every night.** `checkNoRecentSends` treated "0 sends AND overdue pending" as a fault, but overnight and at weekends that is the correct state — campaigns are outside their send window and the backlog is simply tomorrow's queue. Because `schedulerService` already requires `campaignWatchdogService`, importing back would have closed a cycle, so the predicates moved to a new `campaignSendWindow.ts` that both import (CLAUDE.md Modular Composition Rule). Evaluated per campaign against each campaign's own `send_time_start/end` + `send_active_days`, not one global business-hours guess. **(3) The security scan could never scan anything.** `CodeSecurityAuditAgent` mixed tree-walking, regex matching, and DB ticket-writing in one module, so it could only run where a database existed — but the production image ships only compiled `dist` with no TypeScript source. The pure scan is extracted to `scanners/codeSecurityScan.ts` (no DB, no I/O beyond reading files); the agent calls it with identical behaviour, and a new `scripts/runSecurityScan.ts` + CI job runs the **same** scan (not a reimplementation that could drift) where the repo is actually checked out.

Jest: **3 suites, 34 tests, all passing** — new `campaignSendWindow.test.ts` (13 tests) covers the exact boundaries that decide signal vs noise: inside mid-morning, **outside overnight** (the false-alarm case), outside at weekends during business hours, both window boundaries inclusive, one minute past close exclusive, fail-open on a malformed timezone so a config typo cannot halt all sending, per-campaign override beating the default, and `call_timezone` fallback. - [x] **Hotmail auto-archive fixed: it was wired to the Graph client production has no credentials for**
  - Date: 2026-08-15
  - Session: CC-20260814-k4m9
  - What changed: Found while clearing 281 Cory alert emails out of Ali's Hotmail inbox by hand — the inbox should never have filled up, because `autoArchiveService` is supposed to file AUTOMATION mail automatically. It was logging `MS Graph not configured — cannot archive Hotmail message` on every attempt while Hotmail *sync* worked fine in the same process, which is the tell. Two Graph clients exist in this codebase: `msGraphService` (confidential client, requires `MS_GRAPH_CLIENT_ID` + `MS_GRAPH_CLIENT_SECRET` + `MS_GRAPH_TENANT_ID` + `MS_GRAPH_REFRESH_TOKEN` via MSAL) and `graphMailService` (public client, requires only `MS_GRAPH_CLIENT_ID` + `MS_GRAPH_REFRESH_TOKEN`, no secret). Production provisions the **public** pair only — `MS_GRAPH_CLIENT_SECRET` and `MS_GRAPH_TENANT_ID` are absent — so `msGraphService.isConfigured()` returned false on every call. `autoArchiveService` was hard-wired to that one at import time, so every Hotmail archive silently no-opped; `inboxSyncService` reads through `graphMailService` and therefore worked, which is why the mismatch never looked like a Graph problem. Archiving now resolves the client **at call time**, preferring the confidential client when fully provisioned and falling back to the public one, so it works under either credential setup rather than assuming. The failure log now names which specific env vars are set vs missing instead of a bare "not configured", and a module that genuinely fails to load is logged rather than swallowed by a bare `catch {}` — that swallow made a broken import indistinguishable from "not configured" and is why this took months to surface.
  - Verification: `tsc --noEmit` clean at the repo's pinned TypeScript 5.7.3. New `autoArchiveGraphClient.test.ts`: **4 tests, all passing** — the production shape (confidential unconfigured + public configured → public client used), confidential preferred when both are available, clean skip when neither is configured, and no throw when the chosen client errors (archive is explicitly non-critical). The public client was independently proven to work against the live mailbox during the manual cleanup: 281 messages moved with zero failures using exactly the credentials `msGraphService.isConfigured()` was rejecting.
  - Notes: **`replyDraftService` has the same wiring bug and is NOT fixed here.** It throws `MS Graph not configured — cannot send Hotmail reply` for the same reason, but `graphMailService` exports no send function (only `fetchInboxMessages`, `fetchFolderMessages`, `archiveMessage`), so making Hotmail replies work needs a new public-client send implementation rather than a one-line rewire — a bigger change that did not belong in this fix. Sending Hotmail replies remains broken. Also worth noting the manual cleanup was a **move to Deleted Items, not a purge** (Graph `DELETE` is a move), with a full manifest of all 281 message ids/subjects/timestamps saved to `/root/hotmail-purge-manifest-20260815.json` on the prod host before anything was touched.

Root cause is **not** the videos and **not** the timeline code — it is `nginx/security-headers.conf`. PR #1443 (`2cf5e629`, 2026-08-13) fixed a genuine nginx bug: `add_header` is inherited from an outer block only when the inner block declares none of its own, so several `location` blocks that set their own cache-control headers were silently discarding every server-level security header — including `location /`, the SPA fallback serving the entire site. That fix was correct and made the CSP reach browsers **for the first time**, having been configured but inert since before the 2026-07-09 launch-readiness audit. The policy it started enforcing says `frame-src 'self' data: blob:`, which allows no video provider at all, while `frontend/src/utils/videoEmbed.ts`'s `parseVideoUrl()` renders every video as an iframe to `youtube-nocookie.com` (or `player.vimeo.com` / `loom.com` / `fast.wistia.net`). So the moment the header went live, every video iframe in the product was blocked. `frame-src` now lists exactly the hosts the app embeds. **A second, independent defect found in the same audit:** the policy declared no `media-src` at all, so `<audio>`/`<video>` fell back to `default-src 'self'` — which blocked the 24 Buzzsprout podcast episodes and every direct-file `.mp4` card, a surface that would still have been broken after fixing `frame-src` alone. `media-src 'self' data: blob: https:` is now explicit. Both directives carry comments naming the code that depends on them so the next tightening pass does not silently repeat this.
  - Verification: Root cause proven live, not inferred — `curl -D -` against `https://enterprise.colaberry.ai/portal/today` returned the CSP with `frame-src 'self' data: blob:` and **no `media-src` directive present at all**; the prod file at `/opt/colaberry-accelerator/nginx/security-headers.conf` was confirmed byte-identical to the repo's, and `2cf5e629` confirmed an ancestor of the deployed SHA. **The content was independently cleared as healthy**: all 75 distinct YouTube ids across `timeline_cards` were validated against YouTube's oEmbed endpoint and **every one returned 200 — zero dead links**, which is what rules out a content-rot explanation and isolates the CSP as the sole cause. The instant a student collected points (which the UI invites the moment 75% unlocks) `card.status` became `completed`, `done` flipped, `onWatchBeat` went `undefined`, and `VideoEmbed`'s tracking effect early-returns and tears down when `onWatchBeat` is absent. The student watched on to 100% and the stored value stayed at whatever it was when they clicked. **The server was never at fault** — `watchProgressMath.accumulateWatch` caps at 100, not at the threshold. Fix: a separate `reportBeats = !preview` drives the heartbeat while `live` still gates the gate UI, so a completed card keeps measuring but shows no unlock affordance; `TimelineCard` drops `!done` the same way. The scariest step in the setup gave zero feedback that it had worked, and could not go green until the student happened to push. Deliveries are now recorded **before** we decide whether there is work in them, because the receipt itself is the evidence GitHub can reach us; what the delivery *contained* decides what happens next. Ping is acknowledged, recorded, and explicitly **not** counted as the student's work arriving. Two distinct signals now, and conflating them is what made the old UI unreadable: **any** delivery (a ping, or our own bot push) means the webhook is registered; only a **verified** push means their work is flowing. The block became a three-step checklist — repo connected / webhook registered / pushes arriving — shown at once so the shape of the task is visible up front, using the same checkmark vocabulary as "Done means" on the same page rather than inventing a third idiom. States are honest and distinguishable (done / `Your turn` / `Waiting on GitHub`); the old single grey dot meant nothing in particular. It stays **open** while anything is outstanding, which also closed a friction flagged earlier where `Copy command` sat behind a click on "Set it up" while the Story 000 prompt told students to "find the panel and press Copy command". Once registered it **collapses to one quiet line** — repo, green tick, "last push 2 minutes ago" — with `Change` to edit. `Hide` became `Change`/`Done`: nothing was being hidden. The do-not-commit warning stays loud for exactly as long as the command is on screen, and the command and secret disappear once they are not needed.

### Acceptance criteria match on what they say, not on how the dash was typed (2026-08-15)
- [x] **`normaliseCriterion` hardened against punctuation variance — an em dash in STORY-000's third criterion was silently rejecting students' claims**
  - Date: 2026-08-15
  - Session: CC-20260809-b7k2
  - What changed: **Proven in production today, on the one story every student in the cohort builds.** `COMMAND_CENTER_ACCEPTANCE[2]` is `Trust — no tab shows a number, a connection or a result the project has not actually produced.` and that is a real **U+2014 em dash**. `normaliseCriterion` collapsed whitespace and lowercased but deliberately left punctuation alone, so any student, editor, agent or copy-paste path that turned that dash into `-`, `--` or an en dash landed the claim in `rejected_claims`: the story sat at `submitted`, no points were awarded, and the student was told their claim "does not match any acceptance criterion" — accurate and useless. With ~30 students building STORY-000 this Thursday, the failure was one keystroke away for every one of them. The function now absorbs the transformations an **editor or keyboard** performs on text that means the same thing: **NFC** composition, **dash unification** across `- ‐ ‑ ‒ – — ― − ﹘ ﹣ －` plus `--`/`---` runs and the whitespace around them, **quote and apostrophe unification** across the curly/prime/acute family, **ellipsis** `…`→`...`, **invisible debris** (BOM, zero-width space, soft hyphen, word joiner, bidi marks), and **one** terminal period. Both sides of every comparison already route through this single function — `decideStory` normalises `spec.acceptance` and the claim, `mergeProgressFile` normalises the prior and rendered text — so there is no mirror-image bug where only the student's side is forgiven; that was checked rather than assumed. Nothing about what gets WRITTEN changed: `renderProgressFile` still copies plan text verbatim, so `repoWriter`'s content-hash idempotency is untouched.
  - Verification: **The tests were run against the OLD implementation first and watched to fail** — a test nobody has seen fail proves nothing, and that lesson had already cost this workstream once today. New `backend/src/services/sbp/verification/__tests__/criterionIdentity.test.ts`: **21 failed / 19 passed before the fix, 40 passed / 40 after.** The split is the point — the 21 that failed are every typing variant (each dash codepoint asserted individually, smart-vs-straight quotes, trailing period, a Word round trip, invisible debris, NFC-vs-NFD); the 19 that passed **before and still pass after** are the safety half, so the fix is proved not to have loosened them. The criterion text is read from the shipping `COMMAND_CENTER_ACCEPTANCE` constant, not retyped, and a guard test asserts it still contains an em dash. Every dash codepoint in both the test and the implementation was dumped and confirmed byte-for-byte rather than eyeballed. Full SBP suite **41 suites / 757 tests** green. `tsc --noEmit` at the **pinned TypeScript 5.7.3** reports only the 4 pre-existing `Cannot find module 'playwright'` errors (playwright is neither installed nor a declared dependency in this repo; none of the files touched here import it) — zero errors in anything this change touched, and the new test file, which `tsconfig` excludes, was typechecked separately and is clean. Frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean.
  - Notes: **The line held: forgiving about how the text is TYPED, never about what it SAYS.** Dashes and quotes are UNIFIED, never deleted, which is what keeps `read-only` distinct from `read only` and `the label is "sample"` distinct from `the label is sample`. **NFC, never NFKC** — NFKC is compatibility folding and would fuse `x²` onto `x2` and `½` onto `1/2`, which are different claims about a system. `?` and `!` are not stripped even though `.` is: "the API returns 200" and "the API returns 200?" are a claim and a question. Also deliberately refused: backticks (no keyboard substitutes `` ` `` for `'`), guillemets, commas/colons/slashes (`10:00` vs `1000`), ZWJ (load-bearing inside emoji sequences), a leading `- ` list bullet (out of scope, and refusing it can only withhold a match, never invent one), and anything resembling stemming or a similarity score. **The regression that matters most is pinned explicitly: a reworded or paraphrased criterion still lands in `rejected_claims` and still does not verify** — including a paraphrase that keeps most of the words (`…the project did not produce`), a dropped prefix, a dropped clause, and a negation, each asserted as a non-match. A student cannot pass by claiming a criterion they did not meet. Also fixed: `frontend/.../useStoryVerification.ts` carried a comment claiming it "mirrors the backend's `normaliseCriterion`", which this change made false. It is **not** on the gating path — it diffs plan text against plan text from the same response, for deciding which boxes render ticked — so the comment now says what it actually does and why duplicating the matcher into the frontend would only create a second copy to drift. **Not merged, not deployed** (PR opened for review); no student row, no backfill, no emails.

### Schema post-check stops crying wolf about a column that exists (2026-08-16)
- [x] **assertSbpSchema column query derives its table list from REQUIRED_COLUMNS instead of a hardcoded pair**
  - Date: 2026-08-16

The component now pins its own box (`padding:0`, `boxSizing`, `lineHeight:0`, `flex:none`). **The real defect was the assumption, not the padding** — a component shared across three composers cannot assume the absence of host styles. A missing glyph reads as whitespace, so it went unnoticed for years — it surfaced only because an attach button with no text label appeared as an empty square. Fixed by adding the dependency and importing its CSS (3 files, 29 lines, **zero call sites touched**), chosen over rewriting 546 call sites to `ri-*`, which would have meant hand-mapping 162 icon names in a diff reviewable only by trusting the author. Imported from npm rather than a CDN for the reason `public/index.html` already records for the web fonts: no third-party request per page load, and no third-party outage that silently erases the UI's iconography. `package-lock.json` updated in the same commit because the nginx Dockerfile uses `npm ci`, which fails hard on a drifted lockfile.

That last step is the one that matters here: this repo has a documented history of nginx's static-asset location intercepting paths and serving the wrong thing, so "present in the image" is not "reachable by a browser". For #1515 the box-pinning styles were confirmed verbatim in the served bundle (`padding:0,boxSizing:"border-box",lineHeight:0,flex:"none"`).

### The 30-hour inbox watcher: bounded, expiring, and unable to answer its own mail (2026-08-16)
- [x] **T9 of loop-architect run `20260816-student-unblock-and-watch` — autonomous inbox watcher built, gated, and NOT started (PR [#1540](https://github.com/ColaberryIntern/ColaberryEnterprise_AI_LeadershipAccelerator/pull/1540))**

An independent audit scored the plan's first version 10/20 and named T9 specifically: "no poll interval, no per-thread or total reply cap, no dry-run default, no mechanical expiry and no named kill command, and inherits none of the loop guards the repo already pinned after the 2026-07-14 self-reply storm." Every one of those is now a mechanism with a test behind it. New `backend/src/services/inbox/watcher/` (9 modules) plus the runner `backend/src/scripts/runInboxWatcher30h.ts`. **Guards reused, not rewritten:** `resolveDryRun`, `normalizeEmailAddress` and `coraAutoReplySkipReason` are imported from `coraAgentService.ts`, so the self-address / bounce / no-reply / RFC-3834 / bulk-precedence guards that incident produced are inherited rather than reimplemented and left to drift. **Mechanical expiry:** `watch-window.json` stores the start instant and a precomputed `expires_at`, re-read every cycle — a restart adopts the original deadline instead of getting a fresh 30 hours, and every unreadable-clock branch (missing, corrupt, bad date, clock moved backwards) resolves to expired, never to active. **Ceilings:** 1 per thread, 2 per recipient, 15 per window, counted from an fsync'd JSONL log rather than process memory so a restart cannot reset them; the `reply_attempt` record is written *before* the provider call so a crash under-sends rather than double-sends. Breaching a ceiling escalates to Ali, it never silently drops. **Dry run is the default** (`WATCHER_DRY_RUN` must be exactly `"false"` to send, borrowed verbatim from Cora's rule). **Poll interval** 300s, floored at 30s so a mistyped `0` cannot become a hot loop. **Kill switch:** `touch <run-dir>/WATCHER-HALT`, checked at the top of every cycle *and* again immediately before every send, with the send harness's own `HALT` file honoured too and an unreadable state dir counted as halted. **The seam with the send harness (PR #1536):** Ali is BCC'd on all 25 sends, so 25 copies of our own outbound land in the mailbox being watched. Identification uses the harness's send-ledger message ids **and** its `X-Colaberry-Outbound-Copy` header, compared after normalising angle brackets and case; when the two disagree the watcher reports the seam as broken and drops to escalate-only rather than letting whichever side answered win. A missing or corrupt ledger does the same — corrupt lines are refused, not skipped, because a half-written record is exactly where a sent message id goes missing. **Auto-reply is limited to four classes and exactly one repair is ever applied automatically** (minting a fresh sign-in link: reversible, idempotent, touches no student work, provable by re-reading the row). Everything else is diagnosis-only. `claimGate.ts` is the honesty control: a sentence may appear in a reply only if named evidence backs it, a *fix* claim additionally needs evidence gathered after the change with a timestamp proving it postdates the write, the gate checks each verified claim actually appears in the body being sent, and it refuses a body asserting a repair no claim supports. Money, refunds, withdrawals, anything destructive, Ikenna, both Marione addresses, the four students holding the 24 hand-ticked completions, an ambiguous multi-class message and an unclassifiable one all escalate to Ali by email plus `emitAlert`. A student whose address resolves to more than one active enrollment gets no link — that is the Million Meshesha failure, and the watcher does not guess which seat to mint against. `scripts/cron-env-wrapper.sh` gains `GMAIL_*` in its env allowlist (additive; no existing job can break on it) — without it the watcher would start, poll, classify and then fail at the send, which is the silent-no-op shape that allowlist should never cause.
  - Why: Ali, verbatim — "watch my email for the next 30 hours where if they reply with a problem, you can assess, fix and then email reply back to them."

Production is on `7c60a7b6` and untouched.** Starting it requires, in order: PR #1536 (the send harness + ledger) merged and the 25 emails actually sent, because the watcher reads `send-ledger.jsonl` from the run directory and drops to escalate-only without it; `scripts/cron-env-wrapper.sh` copied to the VPS if it is to run under host cron; a first invocation with `--run-dir` pointed at the SAME directory the send used. **It must run host-side on the machine holding the run directory** — nothing is mounted from the host into the backend container, so an in-container run cannot see the ledger at all. Recommended mode is `--once` on a 5-minute crontab rather than one long-lived 30-hour process: a cron tick reads its deadline off disk each time and survives an OOM kill or a dropped session, and after expiry every tick is a logged no-op, so a leftover crontab line is harmless. **Honest limits, disclosed not buried:** `webhook_not_firing` is diagnosed from `github_connections.webhook_secret` and `last_sync_at`, which are proxies for registration and last activity, not a true delivery log — the reply states exactly those two readings and claims no repair; `repo_connect` and `project_state` are diagnosis-only because connecting a repo needs the student

### Intern Delivery briefing missed its 08:45 CT slot on a transient Basecamp 401: 401 made retryable, dead token health-check restored to main (2026-08-17)

- [x] **Basecamp 401 is now a recoverable condition in the Intern Delivery harvester, and `bcTokenHealthCheck.sh` — scheduled on prod for ~30 days but never present on disk — is back on main**
  - Date: 2026-08-17
  - Session: CC-20260817-k4m9
  - What changed: Ali reported the Monday 08:45 CT intern briefing never arrived. The cron fired exactly on time; Basecamp rejected it. `/var/log/intern-delivery-briefing.log` shows `matched slot Monday 08:45 CT`, then `0 people on the project roster`, then `FATAL UpstreamUnavailable: GET .../todosets/4327600402/todolists.json -> 401`. **The token was not expired.** Proven, not inferred: `refreshBasecampTokenFromVault.sh` had run at 08:00 UTC that morning with `probe HTTP 200` and `CCPP rows updated: 1`; a read-only audit of `CCPP.Basecamp_AuthInfo` (SHA-256 fingerprints only, never the token) showed the reader resolves row **242** (`IsActive=1`, `ORDER BY BasecampAuthInfoID DESC` — reader and writer agree on the same row, so this was not a row-targeting mismatch) and that row probed **200** live at 14:12 UTC; and the on-disk `bc-token.cache`, rewritten at 13:54 UTC by the next job through the wrapper, fingerprints `37bb9ce51dd5` — **byte-identical to row 242**, i.e. the exact token that had 401'd nine minutes earlier at 13:45. Same token: 200 at 08:00, 401 at 08:45, 200 at 08:54. So the failure was a transient upstream auth rejection, and the actual defect is that `bcFetch()` in `internDeliveryData.js` retried 429 and 5xx but let 401 fall through to the non-retryable branch — one blip killed the whole morning report. Three fixes. **(1) `internDeliveryData.js`:** 401 is now retryable, handling both causes that hide behind it. A new `createTokenSource(initialToken, refreshFn)` holds the token mutably for the run, so a rotation fixes every *subsequent* request too rather than only the retried one; `refresh()` resolves `true` **only when the value actually changed**, so a resolver that hands back the same string falls through to backoff instead of instantly replaying an identical request; concurrent 401s collapse into one CCPP round trip via an in-flight promise; refreshes are capped (`MAX_TOKEN_REFRESHES=2`) so a genuinely dead token fails fast as `AuthError` instead of hammering CCPP; a resolver that throws degrades to backoff and is never itself fatal. 401 gets its own longer curve (`[5s, 20s, 45s]`, separate from the 429 curve) because auth blips here clear in minutes, not milliseconds. `token` was threaded as a bare string through 23 sites; those internals now take the auth source (`bcGet`/`bcGetAll`/`collectListTodos`/`collectComments` are module-private, so no external contract moved). **(2) `sendInternDeliveryScheduled.js`:** passes a `refreshToken` callback that force-re-reads CCPP, plus `buildFreshSnapshotWithRetry()` — up to 3 whole-harvest attempts 2.5 min apart, gated to retryable `error_class` values only. Inner retry covers ~1 min; this covers the multi-minute case actually observed. Budget is deliberate: cron fires 15 min before the call, worst case lands ~08:53, still ahead of 09:00. **(3) `bcTokenHealthCheck.sh` restored to main.** The daily 13:00 UTC cron `0 13 * * * .../bcTokenHealthCheck.sh` has been logging `/bin/sh: 1: ...: not found` **every day for 30+ days** — the file was added in `221328e3` (2026-06-23) on a branch that `git merge-base --is-ancestor 221328e3 main` proves **never merged to main**; it survives only on four `workstream/*` branches, while its sibling `refreshBasecampTokenFromVault.sh` reached main by another route. Prod deploys main, so the token smoke detector has never once run. Restored from that commit and hardened for exactly the condition just observed: it now **re-probes 30s after a bad result and alerts only if both fail**, because a single-probe detector would page Ali on precisely the transient 401 documented above. It is also committed **mode 100755**: `git ls-tree 221328e3` shows the original was stored `100644`, so even if that branch had merged, `git pull` would have created a non-executable file and the cron would have failed with "Permission denied" instead of "not found" — the same dead detector by a different error string. `refreshBasecampTokenFromVault.sh` was `100644` too (it only works today because someone chmod'd it to 755 on the box by hand on 2026-06-24, a fix that would not survive a fresh clone), so its mode is corrected in the same commit; this is a no-op on the running prod file. **(4)** `refreshBasecampTokenFromVault.sh` printed `CCPP row 237 refreshed` from a hardcoded `CCPP_ROW='237'` constant while its SQL wrote `MAX(BasecampAuthInfoID) WHERE IsActive=1` (row **242** today) — the log has been naming the wrong row on every run since the hardcoded-id bug was fixed. The constant is deleted; the script now SELECTs the target id and reports the row it actually wrote.

Covers happy path, 401→rotate→retry-with-the-new-token, rotation persisting across later requests in the same run, unchanged-token→backoff, the exact 2026-08-17 shape (valid token, 401, 401, 200, no resolver wired), `AuthError` after the cap, the CCPP refresh cap, a throwing resolver, 429/5xx no-regression, and 5 `createTokenSource` unit cases including concurrent-refresh collapsing. - [x] **Loop Architect run — ticket board "takes forever to load," root-caused and fixed: indexes + a real default date filter + DB-side stats aggregation, code-complete and quality-gate green**

  - What changed: Founder reported the ticket board "takes forever to load." Live production `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (16,186 rows) confirmed a real root cause but not the assumed one: `status <> 'done'` does NOT trigger a seq scan for lack of an index (`tickets_status` already exists) — at 32.9% selectivity Postgres correctly prefers a scan over that many scattered heap fetches. The actual defect: `getTicketsForBoard()` (`ticketService.ts`) has no default status filter and no LIMIT, so a normal page load fetches literally every ticket, every column (JSONB `metadata`, TEXT `description`/`summary_current`), every time — confirmed live at ~30MB of Postgres row data (width=1897 bytes/row × 16,186 rows) marshaled into JS objects and shipped to the browser on every open, growing ~500+/week from agent activity alone. Fixed the actual bottleneck, not a plausible-sounding one: (1) new idempotent `backend/src/db/ensureTicketIndexesSchema.ts` — `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_tickets_created_at ON tickets (created_at)` + `idx_tickets_status_created_at ON tickets (status, created_at)`, wired into `server.ts`'s boot sequence (`ensureCommunicationIndexes()` precedent — `CONCURRENTLY` because `tickets` is write-heavy, 16+ autonomous agents inserting continuously); (2) `getTicketsForBoard()`/`getTicketById()` gained an additive, optional `createdAfter` filter (`Op.gte` on `created_at`), parsed server-side from a new `created_after` query param on both `/api/admin/tickets` and `/api/admin/tickets/board` (malformed/absent → silently ignored, never a 400 — a display filter, not a required contract field); (3) the frontend (`AdminTicketBoardPage.tsx`) now defaults to `dateRange:'recent'`, sending `created_after=<7-days-ago ISO>` on every load, with an explicit "Last 7 Days"/"All Time" segmented toggle that composes with the existing Priority/Type/Source dropdowns and the 2026-08-17 clickable stat cards (not a parallel filter system) — deliberately NOT reset by "Clear"/Total (a view-mode choice, not a dropdown filter), plus an honesty banner ("N older tickets hidden — Show all") so the 7-day default never silently reads as "this is everything." `/api/admin/tickets/stats` stays global/unscoped by design (Assumption 2 — KPI cards are whole-system truth, matching how they already ignore Priority/Type/Source). Investigated and found NOT broken, left untouched: the batched actor-name resolver (`resolveActorDisplayNamesBatch`, 32 distinct pairs/request) and the per-request auto-check resolver (`buildTicketAutoCheckResolver`, built once per request, applied in-memory per ticket) — both already correctly batched from the 2026-08-17 work, zero N+1 found. Alert policy is deterministic and idempotent: passing runs send nothing (no-noise rule), a failing run sends at most ONE email per UTC day keyed on `(date, kind)` in an atomically-written state file, and the first pass after a failure sends exactly one "back to green" notice so silence always means green rather than "the monitor died again". - [x] **Security scan: fix the SQL heuristic that was 93% false positives**
  - Date: 2026-08-18
  - Session: CC-20260814-k4m9
  - What changed: Triaged the report-only baseline shipped in #1472 rather than leaving 243 findings unreviewed. Of 229 "critical SQL injection" hits, **213 were noise** — 113 `console.log` lines and 100 prompt/SMS/narrative strings. Root cause was the pattern itself: `/`...\$\{...\}...(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|WHERE|FROM)/i` matched a lone keyword, case-insensitively, so ordinary English prose containing "from", "deleted" or "updated" was reported as a critical vulnerability — `console.log(\`Extracted \${n} chars from \${file}\`)` being a representative example. Two changes fix it: drop the `/i` flag (SQL keywords are uppercase in this codebase, English prose is not) and require a full statement SHAPE rather than a lone keyword (`SELECT..FROM`, `INSERT INTO`, `UPDATE..SET`, `DELETE FROM`). A leading lookahead preserves the requirement that the literal is interpolated, since a fully static SQL string carries no injection risk.
  - Verification: `tsc --noEmit` clean at the repo's pinned TypeScript 5.7.3. New `codeSecurityScan.test.ts`: **15 tests, all passing** — 5 assert real interpolated SQL is still caught (SELECT..FROM, INSERT INTO, UPDATE..SET, DELETE FROM, quoted-identifier form), 6 assert specific REAL lines from this codebase that the old pattern wrongly flagged are now clean, and 4 cover boundaries (static SQL ignored, `UPDATED..SETTINGS` not read as `UPDATE..SET`, lowercase prose ignored). Scan re-run against the full tree: **243 findings -> 60** (sql_injection 229 -> 46), and every surviving SQL hit is in a file that genuinely builds SQL (`sqlExecutor`, `dataProfiler`, `localQueryEngine`, `dataAccessService`, `weeklyReportAgent`, two raw-query routes).
  - Notes: **The 46 survivors were checked and none is exploitable.** Most cluster in `localQueryEngine.ts`, which interpolates table and column identifiers — but those come from the `DatasetRegistry` DB table, and the user's free-text question is only used to MATCH against that registry, never to supply a name, so the identifiers are allowlisted by construction; `dataProfiler.ts` additionally wraps them in `escapeId()`. The finding is therefore "the scanner was broken", not "the codebase is vulnerable". Still known-imperfect and deliberately left report-only: the scanner flags **its own pattern-definition file** (`codeSecurityScan.ts:63`, the `eval()` pattern matching the literal string `eval(` inside its own regex), and `data/classTeachWeeks.ts` legitimately contains SQL examples as curriculum content. Both are path/self exclusions worth adding before anyone turns on `--fail-on`.
  - Hazard worth recording: patching this file via a shell heredoc silently wrote **literal 0x08 backspace bytes** wherever `\b` was intended — the regex looked correct in the terminal but was corrupt on disk, and `Edit` could not match it. Caught with `od -c`. This is exactly the failure the repo's own "never write source via shell heredoc" rule warns about.
