### Reese introduces themselves — two intros, and the silent index bug that nearly buried the second (2026-08-18)
- [x] **Reese greets every new account and every new student, live in production; a stale unique index that made the second intro structurally impossible found and fixed (#1574, #1586, #1590, #1594)**
  - Date: 2026-08-18
  - Session: CC-20260815-m4x7
  - What changed: Ali asked for Reese to greet people the first time they get access. Landed across four PRs, two of them corrections to my own work. **(1) #1574 — the first draft**, one intro, led with "I'm Reese, with admissions". **(2) #1586 — Ali's revision**, and the important one: lead with MENTOR, not admissions (Reese's locked persona is the student's AI Systems Architect mentor, and a greeting that said admissions contradicted the persona a student met minutes later — admissions survives in the account intro only, as something Reese can *also* help with), and **two** intros rather than one, because there are two distinct moments: `account` when someone gets a login, `student` when they join a real class. Someone who signs up and later enrols hears from Reese twice. **(3) #1590 — someone already enrolled at first contact gets the class intro ONLY**; two DMs in the same second is noise, and "have a look around, tell me what you want to build" is stale on arrival for someone who has already paid. The account slot is RETIRED (`outcome='superseded'`) rather than skipped, so that stale message can never surface on a later login. **(4) #1594 — the defect below.** Mechanics: the ledger `reese_welcomes` does double duty, because enrollments carry no `last_login_at` — the ABSENCE of a row is what defines a first login. Rows are CLAIMED BEFORE the send, so the unique index rejects the loser of a concurrent-login race (two tabs, phone and laptop) before it can send a duplicate. Messages are DETERMINISTIC, not LLM-generated: this is the first thing a person ever hears from Colaberry, it is identical for everyone, and generating it would add latency to the login path and per-person cost for a fixed string. Fired from `verifyMagicLink`, `createFreeAccount` and `selectCohort`, always fire-and-forget — nothing here may break a login. Deliberately NOT gated on `reeseEligibilityService`'s pilot cohort: that gates autonomous OUTREACH (Reese deciding on its own to chase someone), and greeting an arrival is a different act. `REESE_WELCOME_ENABLED=false` is the kill switch.
  - Verification: 29 tests on the welcome service, 140 across all of `services/reese`; every merge green on all six CI checks including the `Frontend build` gate. **Verified live in production after deploy, and that verification is what found the defect** — `reese_welcomes` carried BOTH `idx_reese_welcomes_enrollment_once UNIQUE (enrollment_id)` (the single-intro release's index) and the new `idx_reese_welcomes_enrollment_kind_once UNIQUE (enrollment_id, kind)`. The narrower one caps each person at ONE row, so the student intro's insert was rejected by the database, the service read that rejection as "already sent" (the correct reading for a lost race), and the class message would simply never have arrived — **no error, no log, nothing to notice**. The second intro was structurally impossible in any environment that had booted the earlier release. Dropped by hand on prod (2 rows intact); #1594 adds the `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS` so every other environment self-heals on boot. Two real account intros confirmed sent end to end.
  - Notes: **A statement I made to Ali became false and I did not re-check it.** I verified the admissions version was merged-but-not-deployed and told him nobody had received it. Another session deployed the backend shortly after, and `millionabate19@gmail.com` received the admissions-worded greeting at 21:47 UTC before the revision landed; `kes@colaberry.com` correctly received the mentor-led version at 22:42. On a repo where concurrent sessions deploy all day, "not deployed" is a reading with a shelf life, not a fact. **The student intro has never fired** — prod shows `account: 2`, `student: 0`, since nobody has joined a class since deploy. It is proven by tests only; the next enrolment is the real exercise. **Root cause worth carrying:** this repo's idempotent `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` ensure-script pattern is add-only by design — excellent at converging a NEW table, blind to a CHANGED one. Any future ensure-script that changes an existing index must drop the old one explicitly, because it will otherwise survive alongside and silently enforce the old rule.

- [x] **Security scan: documented file exclusions, reported rather than silent**
  - Date: 2026-08-19
  - Session: CC-20260814-k4m9
  - What changed: Follow-on to #1591, closing the two known imperfections that made `--fail-on` unsafe to enable. The scanner was flagging **its own pattern-definition file** (its `eval()` rule contains the literal string `eval(` inside its own regex, so it reported itself every run — a false positive impossible to fix in place) and `data/classTeachWeeks.ts`, which is curriculum content whose SQL and JavaScript snippets are lesson data shown to students, never executed. Added an `EXCLUDE_FILES` list carrying a REASON per entry, matched on exact repo-relative path rather than a glob, plus an exported `isExcludedFile()`. Excluded files are skipped BEFORE the scanned counter increments, so coverage is not overstated, and `CodeScanResult` now carries `filesExcluded` which `runSecurityScan.ts` always prints — an exclusion list that hides what it skipped is how a scanner quietly stops covering real code while still reporting a clean run.
  - Verification: `tsc --noEmit` clean at the repo's pinned TypeScript 5.7.3. Test suite grown to **20 tests, all passing** (15 from #1591 plus 5 new): the two intended files are excluded, ordinary application code is NOT (`graphMailService`, `localQueryEngine` explicitly asserted), matching is exact so a lookalike path (`classTeachWeeksHelper.ts`, `other/classTeachWeeks.ts`) is still scanned, and Windows separators normalise. Scan re-run end to end: **60 -> 55 findings**, with the two exclusions and their reasons printed above the results.
  - Notes: **A test caught a real defect during this change.** `isExcludedFile` originally normalised with `split(path.sep)`, which is a no-op on Linux where `path.sep` is already `/` — so a Windows-style path would never have matched, and the exclusion would have silently failed in CI. Replaced with an explicit `replace(/\/g, '/')` that normalises both separators regardless of platform. The cross-platform test was written before the implementation was checked, which is why it surfaced rather than shipping.

From that moment `reconcileProjects`' `matchIdx` matches, so the `supersede` branch — guarded by `matchIdx < 0 && mirrorIdx < 0` — is unreachable in exactly the case it was written for. **The brief's stated follow-on mechanism was inverted and the corrected one matters:** overlay was *not* a no-op. `generateSkeleton`'s template tasks carry **no `storyId` at all** (`id: '<localId>-t<n>'` and nothing else), so the template's keys and the plan's `STORY-NNN` keys are wholly **disjoint** — `adoptServerTasks` therefore **added** the plan to the template instead of replacing it. The card became the union, ten generic tasks plus the real stories, still `origin: 'local'`. That is exactly the 27 and 29 measured in the browser against published plans of 17 and 19 stories: **10 + 17 and 10 + 19**. Fix: decide supersede on whether the row *is* this plan, using task identity, which is the only thing ids can no longer answer. New pure helper `sharesNoTaskIdentity(p, tree)` — a row sharing **at least one** task key with the tree is this plan (possibly stale, possibly missing a story) and is adopted/overlaid, never superseded; a row sharing **nothing** is the placeholder and the plan supersedes it. New `supersededBy()` carries the placeholder's `legacyIds` (and its own prior id) onto the server plan so bookmarked `/workspace/:id` URLs still resolve through `canonicalProjectId`. **D1.** "Active builds" rendered `projects.length`, and `read()` re-seeds `sample-salon` whenever it is missing, so the number was one too high at every value (0→1, 1→2, 2→3) — the "Active builds: 2 while the API returned 1" report was a training fixture counted as a build the student owns, not a stale cache. ### Secret scanning: full-history sweep + pre-commit and CI prevention (2026-08-19)
- [x] **gitleaks-based secret gate — pre-commit hook, PR check, and weekly full-history sweep, replacing a 5-regex current-tree-only scanner**
  - Date: 2026-08-19
  - Session: CC-20260819-s3k9
  - What changed: This repository is public, so any committed credential is world-readable permanently and is not removed by a later deletion. Prevention added at two layers, both driven by one shared ruleset (`.gitleaks.toml`) so a finding can never pass locally but fail in CI. **Hook:** `.githooks/pre-commit` scans staged content only; wired up by a root `prepare` script (`git config core.hooksPath .githooks`) so every clone gets it on `npm install` with no setup step to forget. **CI:** new `.github/workflows/secret-scan.yml` with two jobs — `pull-request` scans the commits a change adds (blocking, on every PR and push to main), `full-history` sweeps all refs weekly and on demand, which is what catches a secret that was committed then deleted. **Binary provisioning:** `scripts/ensure-gitleaks.js` resolves a version-pinned gitleaks (8.30.1) via `GITLEAKS_PATH` → `PATH` → `.git/tools/` cache → GitHub release download with a pinned SHA-256 verified before use; it fails closed, so a missing scanner refuses the commit rather than passing it unscanned. `scripts/secret-scan-run.js` gives the same scan by hand on any OS (`npm run secrets:scan` / `:tree` / `secrets:history`). **Ruleset:** extends the ~180 upstream rules rather than replacing them, plus four repo-specific rules (database/broker connection URI with inline password, Mandrill key, Basecamp token, high-entropy value assigned to a credential-named variable). Deliberately does **not** exclude `docs/`, `*.md` or test files — the previous scanner skipped exactly the places a pasted credential hides; only generated, vendored and binary content is excluded. **Escape hatches, documented in `docs/SECRET_SCANNING.md`:** inline `gitleaks:allow` and `.gitleaksignore` fingerprints are both committed and therefore code-reviewed; `git commit --no-verify` and `SKIP_SECRET_SCAN=1` unblock locally but do **not** skip CI, so nothing reaches main unscanned. The existing `scripts/secret-scan.js` is left untouched and still runs in the `guards` job as a fast smoke test.
  - Verification: **Gate proven against a planted fake credential, not asserted.** A throwaway file carrying a synthetic AWS key and a synthetic Postgres URI was staged and committed: the hook blocked it (`leaks found: 2`), the commit was refused, and `git log` confirmed HEAD unchanged at `19c1bd96`. Planted file then removed; `git status` clean before the real commit. Ruleset separately confirmed to catch a real credential class the previous scanner missed (`gitleaks dir` over the offending script → `leaks found: 1`, where `scripts/secret-scan.js` returns clean — it has no database-URI or generic-assigned-secret rule). Bootstrap verified end to end on Windows: downloaded, checksum-matched, cached under `.git/tools/`, and re-resolved from cache on the next run. **Full-history sweep executed:** 3,671 commits / 133.48 MB scanned, findings triaged by class; triage was done with values redacted at 100% throughout and liveness established by digest comparison, never by printing a value.
  - Notes: The history sweep found one credential that is **live in production** and one already-public class that is **dead/synthetic**. Details, affected paths and rotation status are deliberately **not** recorded here, because this file is itself public — they were reported to Ali directly and rotation is tracked out-of-band. The CI check reports failure but is not yet a *required* status check; making it required needs a one-time branch-protection change (Settings → Branches → `main` → add `Secret scan / Scan new commits`), which is a repo-admin action outside this PR and is called out in `docs/SECRET_SCANNING.md`. Not merged, not deployed; no production writes were made.

Activation now routes through the shared `activateByRef`, which also fixes two silent side-defects of the raw path: it never converted Explorer → paying member (the exact access problem this job exists to heal) and never anchored the billing period on the class start date. Write ordering flipped so the enrollment `paysimple_payment_id` link — the field that removes a candidate from the next run — is written LAST, and the whole per-candidate mutation is wrapped so one failure leaves that candidate fully re-runnable and does not abort the run for everyone else (`linkFailures` in the summary). **(2)** Path A matched on customer id alone: no amount, no time window, while path B had all three and the file header already *documented* the origin guard as covering both. A second, independent copy of the same unscoped query lived in `timelineGatingService.loadGlobalCards`, so the lock context was computed over a different card set than the one rendered. Fix: new leaf module `backend/src/services/timeline/curriculumScope.ts` owning one WHERE (`globalCurriculumWhere()`) plus its pure predicate form (`isSharedCurriculumProgram`), built on the already-canonical, already-test-asserted `CANONICAL_PROGRAM_ID` from `backend/src/data/weekBlueprints.ts`. Legacy rows with `program_id IS NULL` stay in scope, so the result set narrows by exactly one thing: cards that explicitly declare a different program. Files: `curriculumScope.ts` (new), `timelineService.ts`, `timelineGatingService.ts`, `timelineProgramScope.test.ts` (new).

Baseline run: **3 failed, 3 passed, 6 total**. The 3 that passed on `main` are deliberate guard rails (the canonical program is still admitted, legacy NULLs are still admitted, published/active/non-cohort is still enforced) and they still pass after the change, pinning behaviour the fix must not disturb. After the fix, same file: **6 passed, 6 total, exit 0**. `tsc --noEmit` clean, exit 0, using pinned TypeScript **5.7.3** (a bare `npx tsc` in `/backend` resolves a stale 4.9.5 here and both invents and hides errors). Production impact measured before and after by direct query against `accelerator_prod`, read-only: 23 published DOL cards disappear from the student feed (week 1: 8, week 2: 7, week 3: 8), 0 Accelerator cards are affected, and all 135 `program_id IS NULL` rows are already `visibility='archived'` so the NULL allowance admits nothing in production today.

Those 19 completions now point at cards the student can no longer see. Cleaning that up is a data decision for Ali, not something to do unilaterally, and it is deliberately left open. **One adjacent defect found and deliberately NOT fixed here, to keep this diff approvable on its own evidence:** `composer/publishService.ts:17-32` (`toCardInput`) never sets `program_id`, so every card published through the Composer is written with `program_id = NULL` — the sibling `publishNewVideoCards` at line 113 does pass it, which is what shows this is an oversight rather than intent. Combined with the NULL allowance this fix retains for backward compatibility, a *future* second program published through the Composer would leak through the new guard the same way. CI is unaffected: it runs `npm install` (not `npm ci`) at root then backend, and `npx tsc` inside `backend/` resolves the correct compiler. **Separately found, not fixed:** `backend/package-lock.json` is out of sync with `package.json` — `jest`/`ts-jest` are declared in devDependencies but absent from the lock, so `npm ci` cannot install them. CI's use of `npm install` everywhere hides this, but it breaks any lockfile-faithful install.

The three determinism assertions are the load-bearing ones: `repoWriter` decides whether to commit by comparing content hashes, so a single wall-clock stamp in the rendering would turn every sync into a fresh commit on a student's repo forever; the module takes `uploadedAt` as a parameter and reads no clock, and the tests pin byte-identical output across runs, across arrival order, and with no timestamp of its own. The index can only be correct if it sees everything; unchanged files are filtered by content hash before any network call so it costs one API read; and it means a student whose repo was disconnected for three weeks repairs on their next successful sync rather than staying permanently short. **Known and not introduced here:** jest reports "a worker process has failed to exit gracefully" on these suites — an open handle in the imported module graph, not a test failure, and present before these files existed.   - What changed: Thirteen PRs, each already individually approved by Ali, could not be merged. `.gitattributes` sets `PROGRESS.md merge=union`, and **git honours merge drivers locally only** — GitHub does not run them server-side, so it computes mergeability with a plain three-way merge and reported `CONFLICTING` for every PR whose PROGRESS.md region had also moved on `main`, while each one merged perfectly cleanly in a worktree. Clearing that state requires pushing to the branch, and `main` protection sets both `dismiss_stale_reviews` and `require_last_push_approval`, so the push permanently destroys the approval that made it mergeable. It already cost #1618 its approval, and force-pushing back to the previously approved SHA did not restore it. The available credential is the author of all thirteen and cannot self-approve, so the only lawful exit was to compose all thirteen onto `integration/thirteen-approved-prs` and take **one** new approval instead of paying the approval cost thirteen times. `--admin` was never used: the block is a missing human approval, not a failing check. **Root cause addressed in the same change, rather than left to recur:** the `merge=union` line is kept, because it genuinely resolves local PROGRESS.md merges and is what let this composition merge cleanly, but its comment claimed it "eliminates the recurring PROGRESS.md merge conflicts ... which were blocking ~6 of 9 open PRs" — which is false, and is the reason nobody caught this earlier. The comment now states plainly that the attribute is local-only, that a PR can merge cleanly in a worktree and still be blocked in the UI, and what the push actually costs. `MERGE_WORKFLOW.md` gains a "PROGRESS.md conflicts, and why GitHub still says CONFLICTING" section with the diagnosis (including that **a `CONFLICTING` PR reports no checks at all**, which renders almost identically to checks still pending), the merge-main-into-branch fix, the approval cost, and the practical guidance to merge `main` in *before* requesting review while the push is still free. The deeper structural cure — one progress file per session under `docs/sessions/` with `PROGRESS.md` reduced to an index — is **recorded and deliberately not taken**, because it changes a `CLAUDE.md` hard gate and the end-of-session audit protocol, which is a DRI governance decision, not merge plumbing.

Both merges were conflict-free; `git merge-base HEAD origin/main` equals `origin/main` exactly, which is the mechanic that makes GitHub report `MERGEABLE` (main's side of the three-way merge is empty, so the un-honoured merge driver never gets a chance to matter). **The #1624 compile fix still applies and is still load-bearing:** `main` already binds `const drift = summariseUnrecognisedCriteria(...)` from merged #1634, and #1624 binds `const drift = summariseRejectedClaims(...)` in the same function scope (`verifyBuildFromRepo`), giving `TS2451` twice — so **#1624 alone against current main does not compile**, and its green CI reflects a stale base. ### Artifact sync proven in production — and the idempotency defect it exposed (2026-08-21)
- [x] **First real GitHub write confirmed on a Colaberry-owned test repo, which immediately surfaced a defect no unit test could reach: every sync re-committed identical content. Fixed, plus a latent locale-ordering bug found while fixing it.**
  - Date: 2026-08-21
  - Session: CC-20260819-i8it
  - What changed: Deployed the artifact sync to prod (`bb152ded`, backend rebuilt, 0 restarts, compiled `dist/services/artifacts/` verified inside the RUNNING container rather than trusted from the build log) and ran a real end-to-end proof against `ColaberryIntern/AcceleratorTesting` — deliberately a Colaberry-owned repo, never a student's, for the first-ever production write. **The write worked** (commit `0efb1cb8`, `Colaberry Build Bot`, 2 files, one commit): artifact content committed verbatim to `artifacts/week-10/governance-framework.md`, `artifacts/INDEX.md` rendered with the "Built on" column showing the project label, relative link resolving, `chore(colaberry):` prefix present so the push webhook skips its own write. **Then the second run committed again** (`f735f1da`, `outcome:"written"`, same two paths) — the sync was NOT idempotent. Root cause: `repoWriter.changedFiles` compares each file's hash against `.colaberry/manifest.json`, which is written by the PLAN sync and lists only `CLAUDE.md` and `docs/**`; the artifact sync passed a file set containing **no manifest at all**, so artifact paths were compared against entries that did not exist, came back "changed" on every run, and re-committed forever. Fix: new pure `mergeArtifactHashesIntoManifest()` in `artifactRepoFiles.ts` merges artifact hashes INTO the existing manifest (never replaces — dropping the plan's entries would make the next plan sync see all its files as changed and churn in the other direction), and `artifactRepoSync` appends the merged manifest to the file set it writes. **Second, latent bug found while fixing the first:** `localeCompare` was used in 4 places including the manifest serialisation; its result depends on the runtime's ICU data, and everything this module emits is hashed and compared byte-for-byte, so ordering that varies between Node builds is a spurious-diff source. Replaced with a locale-independent `byCodeUnit()` comparator throughout.
  - Verification: **Both defects were found by production evidence, not by tests.** The idempotency bug was proven by two consecutive real syncs producing two distinct commit SHAs on a real repo; the ordering bug was found because a wrong test expectation forced a re-read of the comparator. **Jest 66/66** across both artifact suites (up from 56), including 10 new `mergeArtifactHashesIntoManifest` cases: artifact paths get recorded, plan entries survive untouched, non-`files` fields including `generated_at` are left exactly as found (bumping a timestamp would rewrite the manifest on no-change runs and reintroduce churn from the other end), re-merge updates rather than duplicates, byte-identical on repeat, order-independent, declines rather than fabricating plan bookkeeping when no manifest exists, tolerates unparseable/wrong-shaped input, skips malformed entries, and asserts code-unit rather than locale ordering. Backend `tsc --noEmit` exit 0 (TypeScript 5.9.3, version printed in-band).
  - Notes: **The 21-upload backfill was NEXT on the list and was deliberately NOT run.** Running it before the proof would have put 21 student repos into permanent churn — one bot commit per upload, forever. This is the entire justification for proving on one repo before twenty-one, and it paid for itself on the first attempt. **What the 93 passing tests could not see, and why:** they proved the renderer was deterministic — same inputs, byte-identical output — which was described at the time as the load-bearing property. It was necessary and NOT sufficient. Determinism with nothing persisting the result buys nothing, because the comparison had no record to compare against. The bug lived in the seam between this module and `repoWriter`'s manifest, which no test written against this module could reach. **Known, bounded, documented consequence of the fix:** `renderDocs` rebuilds the manifest from its own file set, so a plan republish drops the artifact entries and the next artifact sync re-commits ONCE — one redundant commit after a republish, not a loop. Making `renderDocs` preserve unknown entries would remove even that; tracked as a follow-up, not silently ignored. **Cosmetic follow-up:** the commit message reads `chore(colaberry): sync build plan — N files` because that string is `repoWriter`'s generic wording; for an artifact commit it names something the commit does not contain, and a student scanning their history sees "build plan" against a governance artifact. **Proof rig still standing and MUST be torn down:** `github_connections` row `aaec4e31-b540-456d-98ed-5dcd476d7d5d`, `runtime_portfolio_artifacts` row `9b7b0320-fc33-4835-82dd-811056ee15ca`, `/app/uploads/proof-governance.md` in the backend container, and the `artifacts/` tree on `ColaberryIntern/AcceleratorTesting`.

### A student's phone can no longer go silent without saying so (2026-08-21)
- [x] **The classroom companion poll stopped swallowing its own failures. Also corrects the root cause recorded in the previous entry, which was wrong.**
  - Date: 2026-08-21
  - Session: CC-20260820-k4m9
  - What changed: `frontend/src/pages/portal/ClassCheckinPage.tsx` polls `companion-state` every 2.5s so the student's phone mirrors whatever is on the instructor's screen. That poll ended in `.catch(() => { /* keep last view */ })`, so **every failure was silent and permanent**: the phone kept rendering its last view forever, with no message, no retry signal and no recovery. `companion-state` is auth-gated (`requireParticipant`), so a dead session produced a phone that looked *exactly* like "the instructor is not on a question slide" - indistinguishable from a working phone, from both the student's end and the instructor's. Now a **401 immediately** shows "You have been signed out" with a sign-in button, because waiting cannot revive a dead session; **anything else** shows "Reconnecting…" only after 3 consecutive failures (~7.5s at the poll interval), which rides out a single dropped request on venue wifi without alarming the room over a blip. Polling continues while disconnected, so recovery is automatic and the student does not have to know to reload. The decision itself is extracted to a pure `frontend/src/pages/portal/classroomLinkState.ts` (following the existing `classroomNextStep.ts` sibling pattern) so it is testable without mounting a page that needs auth context, a router and the portal API client.
  - Verification: new `classroomLinkState.test.ts`, **7 passed** - 401 classified as signed-out immediately and regardless of prior failure count; a single failure and a 503 both stay quiet; silent right up to the threshold and admitting it exactly at it; **a network error with no HTTP status treated as transient rather than as a sign-out**, so an offline phone is never sent to a login screen it cannot reach; never returns `live` past the threshold for any status; and the grace window pinned small enough to matter at a 2.5s poll. Frontend `tsc --noEmit` clean.
  - Notes: **This entry corrects the previous one.** The 2026-08-21 entry above records the cause of the 2026-08-20 incident as the classroom client "trusting the poll keys it loaded with", stranded by a mid-class `kit_config_json` edit renumbering them. **That was wrong.** Poll keys are slide-index derived and a config edit does renumber them, which makes it a tempting story, but `ClassCheckinPage` takes the key straight off each 2.5s response and **there is no client-side key cache to go stale**. The original diagnosis rested on a join-time correlation - the affected student was the earliest joiner - which was real but was over-read into a mechanism that does not exist in the code. The correction was found only by reading the client while implementing the "fix", which is the argument for reading the code you are about to change rather than the code you assume is there. **Honest limit:** the specific error that student hit is still unknown and is not claimed here. Her `portal_token_expires_at` had lapsed on 2026-08-18, but her check-in succeeded at 23:16:51Z, so the magic-link token is probably not what gated her later calls. What is certain is that whatever failed, the phone was built to hide it. The fix is correct for every cause, which is why it was still worth shipping without pinning the exact one. The memory file `reference_never_edit_kit_config_during_class` has been rewritten to name the real defect instead of the invented one; the "finish deck edits before students join" habit survives as caution, not as causation.
### Billing anchor defect: 15 members re-anchored, and the one-line cause fixed (2026-08-21)
- [x] **Found that 15 live subscriptions had their billing clock started on an activation/repair date instead of on the member's payment, repaired all 15 in production, and fixed the line that caused it**
  - Date: 2026-08-21
  - Session: CC-20260821-k4m9
  - What changed: Follow-on from the same session's billing audit. Ali pushed back on the "nothing is due" finding — the class had been running over a month and he expected members to be into a second cycle. He was right, and the first audit was measuring the wrong thing: it read each subscription's stored `current_period_end`, which is itself the broken value. **Root cause is one line: `activateByRef()` calls `billingAnchorMs(nowMs, cohortStart)`, passing the ACTIVATION time into a parameter named `paymentMs`.** When the payment webhook fires promptly, now ≈ the payment date and nothing goes wrong; when a webhook is missed and the row is healed weeks later, the member's billing clock starts at the heal. The 2026-08-12 webhook-backlog repair (`CC-20260812-k4rp`) did exactly that to 13 monthly members, and 2 annual members were hit the same way — 15 total, **202 unbilled days (~$1,300)** given away, with every future renewal permanently shifted later by the same gap. Code fix: `activateByRef` takes an optional `opts.paidAt` and anchors on it, falling back to `nowMs` so the live webhook path is unchanged; `appPaymentReconcileService` (which runs *by design* long after the fact, since it exists to heal missed webhooks) now carries the PaySimple `PaymentDate` it was already fetching through to activation instead of dropping it. New `scripts/repairSubscriptionAnchors.js` — dry-run by default, idempotent, cadence-aware — performs the data repair. Also established on the way past: **`updated_at` on `subscriptions` is NOT trustworthy** (the model sets `timestamps: false`, so it is only written when code passes it explicitly); one member appeared untouched by the repair purely because the old reconciler's raw UPDATE never wrote that column, which briefly looked like a second, separate bug and is not.
  - Verification: Repair ran against production in dry-run first, reviewed row by row, then applied: **13 monthly rows** (Maria C Garcia and 3 others Sep 12/13 → Aug 23, through to Firas → Sep 6) and, after widening scope caught two more, **2 annual rows** (Martin Mungai 2027-07-30 → 2027-07-23, Abrahim Nur 2027-08-12 → 2027-07-27). Post-repair SQL confirms **0 rows still anchored to the repair date and 0 rows overdue**; an immediate re-run reports `planned=0 skipped=30`, proving idempotency. **Two scope guards were added because the widened dry run surfaced real false positives before anything was written:** a 2-day drift floor (10 live rows showed a phantom 1-day delta — SAME calendar due date — because PaySimple reports `PaymentDate` in merchant-local time while our anchors are UTC instants; applying them would have moved real members' deadlines ~23h earlier for nothing), and an ACH exclusion for franck kafando, whose stored anchor is the settlement date rather than the initiation date and is the safer basis. Backend `tsc --noEmit` and `jest` could NOT be run in this environment — `backend/node_modules` here is a partial install with no jest/ts-jest/ts-node and no `@types/node`, so the pinned-5.7.3 typecheck emits 10,866 environment errors (`Cannot find module 'crypto'`, `Property 'findOne' does not exist on type 'typeof Subscription'`) across the whole tree; none of them land on the lines this change adds. **CI is the authoritative gate for this PR and its result is reported on the PR itself.** 3 new regression tests cover the delayed-repair case (paid 7/29, activated 8/12 → anchors 7/29, due 8/29, not 9/12), an early payment recovered late (still anchors on class start), and the fallback when `paidAt` is absent or unparseable.
  - Notes: **Correcting a clock is not the same as collecting the gap** — the 202 unbilled days behind these members are written off, not invoiced, and the script refuses to `--apply` if any computed period end would land in the past. No member was charged and no PaySimple schedule was created. The repair moves 13 members' next payment EARLIER (Maria C Garcia and 3 others to 2026-08-23), so anyone who checked their portal last week saw a later date than they will now see; that is worth a heads-up before the renewal reminders reach them. Separately, **the 09:00 Central renewal-reminder run did not execute today**: another session deployed PR #1686 at 08:45 and the container was still booting at 09:00, which also wiped the `docker cp`'d repair script mid-run (the first apply attempt failed with MODULE_NOT_FOUND and was re-run). The `RENEWAL_REMINDERS_ENABLED` flag survived the deploy because it lives in the host `.env`, and the scheduler re-registered on boot. **Pre-existing and NOT introduced here:** period ends stored just after midnight UTC render as the previous day in Central, so a member whose period ends 2026-08-31 01:00Z is told "paid through August 30" — worth a separate fix. Elizabeth Nzau is anchored to 2026-11-12 (November class start), which is the documented early-pay behavior and was deliberately left alone, though she is paying monthly for a class that has not begun.

So the boxes tick and the number does not move. **The one sentence explaining this was gated on `selfTickedCount > 0`** in `AcceptanceChecklist.tsx` — it rendered only AFTER a tick, so the warning arrived strictly after the mistake it described, and a student who had touched nothing got no explanation whatsoever. Million Abate went four support rounds on exactly this. **Fix, in four parts.** (1) A standing `.rt-acc-note` block, unconditional and placed ABOVE the first row, saying in plain words that a tick is a note saved in this browser, that it confirms nothing, and that the platform confirms each line itself by reading the repo. (2) **The affordance is made honest rather than merely annotated:** an unconfirmed box's `accent-color` moves from `--leaf` to `--muted2`, because leaf green is what "confirmed" means everywhere else on this page (the tag, the verified banner, the header pill), so an unconfirmed box was ticking in the platform's own signal colour. (3) The count now reads "N of M confirmed **from your repo**" — the same three words as the per-row tag — because the previously-correct "0 of 3 confirmed" beside three boxes the student had just ticked reads as a broken scoreboard. Those students are sent to **Get my progress.json** (deployed 18:49 UTC today, on this same page) first. `push` and `null` keep the shorter wording and name no control that may not be rendered. Local ticking is untouched and the "Your note — not confirmed yet" state is kept. Screen readers get the same honesty: unconfirmed rows with no visible tag carry "(your own note, not confirmed)" inside the label, via a new `.rt-sr` class defined in `runtimeCss` rather than borrowing Bootstrap's `.visually-hidden` (this page renders its own chrome, not PortalShell). `.rt-step-h` gains `flex-wrap:wrap` so the longer count cannot overflow at the half-screen width this page is actually used at. ### PaySimple recurring schedules: the capability, with cancellation teardown in the same change (2026-08-22)
- [x] **Built the recurring-billing layer the platform has never had: schedule creation, deterministic recurrence matching in the webhook, storable past_due, and cancellation propagation. No schedules created yet; the migration is a separate reviewed step.**
  - Date: 2026-08-22
  - Session: CC-20260821-k4m9
  - What changed: Ali chose to start automatic billing now, after the same session's audit established the platform has no recurring billing at all (`docs/RECURRING_BILLING_EXPOSURE.md`). New `backend/src/services/paysimpleRecurring.ts` (gateway layer: `createRecurringSchedule` / `getRecurringSchedule` / `suspendRecurringSchedule`, plus a pure `cadenceFor` and `assertStartDateNotPast` that are unit-testable without a network) and `backend/src/services/subscriptionScheduleService.ts` (business rules: exclusions, account resolution, period advance, past_due, teardown, `ensureSubscriptionScheduleSchema`). `subscriptions` gains `paysimple_schedule_id` plus an index, and `SubscriptionStatus` gains `'past_due'` so a failed scheduled charge is **storable** rather than recomputed at read time. **Three design decisions were forced by live probes, not assumed.** (1) `POST /v4/recurringpayment` requires `AccountId`, not `CustomerId`, and our stored `paysimple_customer_id` is the wrong id in every case because the hosted page mints its own customer; the usable account is resolved from the first payment. (2) **A scheduled charge carries `RecurringScheduleId` on the payment object** (confirmed against a live legacy schedule, payment `155927179` / schedule `4434931`), so the webhook matches recurrences deterministically instead of by amount or customer id, which is not unique here (119 subscriptions map to 83 customer ids). (3) Anchor days 29-31 map to `LastofMonth`, never `SpecificDayofMonth: 31`, because eight live subscribers anchor there and that value does not survive a 30-day month. **Cancellation propagation ships in this same change and suspends the schedule BEFORE flipping the local status** - the reverse order would leave a member reading as cancelled in our UI while PaySimple kept drawing their card, which takes money rather than merely failing to. `cancelSubscription` now returns `schedule_suspend_failed` rather than reporting a clean cancellation it did not achieve. Also closed a pre-existing gap flagged in the exposure doc: `paysimpleService.apiRequest` was a bare `fetch` with no timeout; it now has a 30s `AbortController` bound and throws a classified `PaySimpleError` (`TimeoutError` / `RateLimitError` / `AuthError` / `UpstreamUnavailable` / `ValidationError`) instead of a bare `Error`, per the CLAUDE.md external-boundary and error-classification rules.
  - Verification: CI is the gate and its result is on the PR; backend `jest`/`tsc` cannot run in this environment (partial `node_modules`, no jest/ts-jest/`@types/node`). 13 new unit tests across two suites cover the parts that are pure logic and therefore assertable: cadence mapping for mid-month, day 1, day 28 and the 29/30/31 `LastofMonth` cases, annual, and out-of-range rejection; `assertStartDateNotPast` allowing today at any hour and **refusing any past start date**, which is the invariant that stops a migration inventing a catch-up charge; and every exclusion rule, including case/whitespace-insensitive matching and a guard that the two exclusion lists stay disjoint. The webhook recurrence branch and the schedule teardown are integration-shaped (they need a database and a gateway) and are covered by argument, not by test, which is stated here rather than implied. Diff hygiene: an initial blanket em-dash pass rewrote ~51 pre-existing comment lines across four files; those files were reverted to HEAD and the intentional edits re-applied, taking `subscriptionService.ts` from 49/29 changed lines down to 17/1.
  - Notes: **Nothing is scheduled yet and no member is being auto-charged.** This PR is the capability; creating the 25 schedules is a separate step that runs dry-run first and gets its own review, deliberately not bundled with untested code. **The exclusion list is live business state, not a placeholder**: 3 bank-draft members (Britiana Akhile, Kepha Ohanga, franck kafando) are held until they reply "yes" because a recurring ACH series needs affirmative authorization that a one-time web checkout does not cover; Chukwuemeka Eneh is held because his card belongs to a friend in the US who never authorized a recurring series; Shabana Zeeshan is held because her card expired 07/2026. Comp seats are excluded structurally and `createRecurringSchedule` additionally refuses any non-positive amount, so a $0 seat fails loudly rather than reaching the gateway. **Still missing and known:** dunning behavior on top of `past_due` (PaySimple has its own schedule retry policy that must be understood first, or members get two dunning tracks), the migration runner, and a mid-subscription credit path - `startCheckout` is the only place account credit reduces a charge, and a flat schedule amount knows nothing about the credit ledger. **Two open follow-ups from the same session:** our checkout drops any phone that is not exactly 10 digits, which blocks every international member (this is what forced Chukwuemeka onto a friend's card), and period ends stored just after midnight UTC render a day early in Central.

### Artifact backfill run: 1 of 13 synced, and the 12 failures were being told a lie (2026-08-22)
- [x] **Ran the real backfill across every student repo the platform can resolve. One succeeded, twelve failed on write permission — and were told "we'll retry on your next upload", advice that can never come true. Diagnosis and messaging fixed.**

That message is worse than none: only the student can grant push access, so retrying is futile and the one useful instruction went unsaid. New pure module `services/artifacts/writeFailureDiagnosis.ts` — `statusFromMessage()` extracts the embedded HTTP status, `probeRepoReadable()` re-reads the repo after a failed write (never throws; returns null when it cannot establish), and `diagnoseWriteFailure()` separates the two 404 meanings from evidence: **read 200 + write 404 = `no_push_access`; read 404 + write 404 = `repo_missing`; 5xx/429/timeout = `transient`**. When the probe cannot establish either way it falls back to `transient` rather than guessing — sending a student to fix permissions on a deleted repo wastes their time on something they cannot fix. New `repo_gone` outcome on `ArtifactSyncResult`, wired through to `BuildArtifactsRender.tsx` (which previously had no case for it and would have rendered nothing at all).

That is a **6% success rate on the single step every downstream feature depends on**, including the Capstone Record, which would currently have nothing to render for 57 of 58 people. The four planning artifacts treated the week-1 repo connection as a setup step that broadly works; the production data says it does not. ### Curriculum video health: 146 of the 149 "failures" were YouTube refusing to answer (2026-08-22)
- [x] **Fixed the two defects that made the video health check unsafe to switch on, plus the vacuous channel metric. Never enabled the flag and never emitted an alert.**

  - What changed: PR #1698 merged a curriculum video link check that could not be turned on: a `{ dryRun: true }` sweep of 149 videos reported **healthy 0, unknown 0, failures 149**, nearly all with `detail: "Sign in to confirm you’re not a bot"`, while independent oEmbed probes returned 200 for 146 of them. **Defect 1, in `videoLinkClassifier.classify()`:** YouTube reuses `playabilityStatus.status = LOGIN_REQUIRED` for BOTH "this video is private" and "prove you are a person" (and reuses `ERROR` the same way), so the branch `if (status === 'LOGIN_REQUIRED' || oembedStatus === 403) return PRIVATE` read a refusal to answer as an answer, with `actionable: true` on it. The `reason` text was the only discriminator and was being carried as display copy rather than read as signal. Fixed with a new pure `isBotChallenge()` that matches the challenge vocabulary (`not a bot`, `unusual traffic`, `too many requests`, `verify you are human`) against the serialised `playabilityStatus` — deliberately not against a fixed field path, because YouTube has moved that text between `reason`, `messages[]` and the error screen; deliberately NOT matching bare "sign in to confirm", which would swallow age-gating. `readPlayerResponse()` now surfaces `challenged`, and `classify()` short-circuits on it to UNKNOWN **above** every status branch. **Defect 2, the UNKNOWN safety net reading 0:** the net was reachable but wired to the wrong class of event. It guarded `!player.reachable` (we got nothing) and unrecognised signal combinations (we got something strange). A bot challenge is neither — it arrives as HTTP 200 carrying a well-formed player response whose status the classifier recognises with total confidence. The net covered transport failure when the failure mode that actually occurred was a confident answer to a question we were never allowed to ask. **Three further guards, each against a failure mode that actually happened rather than one that seemed likely:** (a) **pacing** — probes were `CONCURRENCY 4` with no spacing, and at ~150 videos x 2 requests throttling is the common case, not the exception (an earlier sweep turned 46 healthy videos "unreachable" this way); now a shared pacer enforces a 350ms minimum gap between any two outbound requests across all workers, with concurrency dropped to 2. (b) **a known-good control in every batch** — each batch of 25 is *bracketed* (before AND after, to catch throttling that starts midway) by a probe of `2xRzYuit9ac`, one of our own videos; if the control does not come back HEALTHY the batch is `untrusted` and **nothing in it may be classified as broken**. Ours on purpose: a third-party control could be made private tomorrow and silently mute the whole check. (c) **two observations before any alert** — every actionable verdict is re-observed in a second, separately controlled burst after a cooldown; a video that fails once and passes on retry is recorded as healthy and never alerts. **Third defect, the channel metric:** `failing_on_our_channel = 0` read as reassurance and was vacuous — `channel` was null for every video, because the watch page carries no microformat for exactly the cases a failure report is about (private, removed, challenged), so the number counted nothing and a boolean `ours` could not say "we could not tell". Fixed both halves: `channel` now falls back to the oEmbed `author_name` where one exists, and `ours: boolean` became `ownership: 'ours' | 'third_party' | 'unknown'` with a three-way breakdown on the run result and in the scheduler log, so an unknown owner can never again be counted as not-ours. New module `services/curriculumHealth/videoLinkProbe.ts` holds the pacer, prober, control and batching (extracted so the service stays about curriculum blast radius; every module is now under the 500-line ceiling, and the service test file was split at the same boundary with shared fakes in `__tests__/helpers/videoLinkFixtures.ts`).

Production was touched **exactly once**, by a single read-only `SELECT` pulling the 159 video-bearing cards; all probing ran from the workstation, so no prod compute, no writes, no deploy, no build. **`dryRun` gating was proven BEFORE the run**, two ways: the single guard `if (!opts.dryRun) {` at videoLinkHealthService.ts encloses both the `emitAlert()` loop and the `setSetting(LAST_RUN_KEY)` write, and the existing unit test asserting both was run green in isolation first; the verification harness additionally rigged `setSetting` and `emitAlert` to **throw**, so a gating leak would have aborted the run loudly rather than quietly writing a last-run key or paging someone. ### The auth-failure alarm stopped crying wolf, and can now name the caller (2026-08-22)
- [x] **Per-event-type spike thresholds, and the real client identity recorded on every auth failure.**
  - Date: 2026-08-22
  - Session: CC-20260820-k4m9
  - What changed: Two halves of one problem, found by pulling on a `[Warning] Error Spike: admin_auth_failed` alert. **1) The alarm was permanently on.** `errorSpikeAlertService` applied ONE global pair (`WARNING_COUNT` 10 / `CRITICAL_COUNT` 25) to all nine watched event types. Measured over the 7 days to 2026-08-22, six of the nine recorded **zero** events, so the default is right for them - but `admin_auth_failed` averaged **48/hr, p95 121, peak 176**, meaning a severity-5/5 critical fired essentially every hour, around the clock, for as long as the data goes back. The alert that finally got investigated reported **46, which is BELOW that baseline**: it was paging on a quiet hour. Added `THRESHOLD_OVERRIDES` + an exported `thresholdsFor()`, with `admin_auth_failed` at 150/250 and `participant_auth_failed` at 30/60 (its own measured peak was 19). Every unlisted type keeps 10/25 exactly. The orchestrator's cheap pre-check used the global constant too, so it was fetching a sample row every run for an alert it then correctly suppressed; it now uses the per-type value. **2) The log could not identify the caller.** Traffic is Cloudflare -> nginx -> Express and `server.ts` sets `trust proxy` to 1, so `req.ip` resolves to the **Cloudflare edge**: a full week of `admin_auth_failed` rows named nothing but `162.159.x` / `172.7x.x`. `authFailureLog` now also records `forwarded_for` and `user_agent` via a new exported `describeCaller()`, wired through all five call sites (`authMiddleware` x3, `participantAuth`, `alumniAuth`).
  - Verification: **33 passed** across `authFailureLog`, `authMiddleware` and `errorSpikeAlertService`. Backend `tsc --noEmit` clean under the backend-local TypeScript 5.9.3 (the root resolves 4.9.5 and reports a false clean). New coverage pins both halves: every unlisted type still returns exactly `{warning:10, critical:25}`; `admin_auth_failed` stays silent at 48, 121 and at the literal 46 from the triggering alert, and still pages at 150/250; `participant_auth_failed` silent at its 19 peak and paging at 30/60; overrides asserted warning-below-critical and never below the shared default, so a future edit cannot silently downgrade one. For the caller fields: the real client is read from the forwarded chain alongside the unchanged edge `ip`, a missing request still yields explicit nulls rather than undefined, a blank header counts as absent, a repeated header arriving as an array takes the first value, and an absurd header is capped at 200 chars so one caller cannot bloat `ai_events`.
  - Notes: **Chose X-Forwarded-For over CF-Connecting-IP after checking `nginx/nginx.conf`**, which sets it explicitly from `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` - so the real caller is the leftmost entry and nothing has to be assumed about which Cloudflare headers survive the hop. **Deliberately additive and deliberately not a trust decision:** `ip` keeps its existing meaning, the new fields sit beside it, and nothing reads them for authorization or rate limiting, so a forged header on a direct-to-origin request misleads a diagnostician at worst. Widening `trust proxy` was considered and rejected: it would make X-Forwarded-For load-bearing and spoofable end to end. **Four existing tests were retargeted, not weakened.** They used `admin_auth_failed` as an arbitrary stand-in for "an auth event type on the default threshold"; since admin now carries an override, they moved to `cory_auth_failed`, same impact area and still on the default, so each test's original intent is preserved exactly. A fifth changed because `logAuthFailure` now receives the request. **The baseline itself is NOT fixed and these thresholds are not an endorsement of it:** something is polling with a dead admin token roughly once a minute, the timestamps cluster at :29-:30 seconds past the minute which is machine cadence rather than human error, and the caller fields exist precisely so the next person can name it. Re-derive the thresholds if that baseline is ever driven down.

  - What changed: Ali reported, with a live screenshot, that a `?creator=...&range=all&status=open` deep link from the AI Organization page started out correctly filtered, then visibly reset to the full unfiltered board a moment later. Root cause: `frontend/src/pages/admin/AdminTicketBoardPage.tsx`'s `filterCreator`/`filterSource`/`filterStatus` used to be set by a SEPARATE `useEffect` that ran AFTER the mount-time `fetchBoard()` effect had already fired once with the still-default (empty) filters. Nothing cancelled that first, unfiltered request, so it raced the correctly-filtered request that followed it - whichever response arrived LAST won the `setBoard()`/`setStats()` call, and the larger unfiltered response (pulling the whole ticket table) frequently arrived after the smaller filtered one over a real network, silently overwriting the correct board a moment after first paint. Fixed by reading every deep-link param (`?open`, `?source`, `?creator`, `?status`, and `?range`, which already used this pattern from the prior fix) synchronously via lazy `useState` initializers off one shared `URLSearchParams` read, instead of a follow-up effect - there is now only ever ONE board fetch on a deep-linked mount, so nothing is left to race. PR #1733, SHA `c15023f7`.
  - Verification: New regression test asserts board-fetch call COUNT (not just the last call's URL) for a `?creator=&range=all&status=open` deep link - proves exactly 1 fetch fires, where the old code fired 2. This is the actual proof the race is gone: every PRE-EXISTING test in this file only ever checked `calls[calls.length-1]`'s URL, which was always correctly filtered by construction (call ORDER, not response ARRIVAL order) - none of them could have caught this bug, which is exactly why it shipped unnoticed. All CI checks passed (`tsc --noEmit` both stacks, backend unit tests, frontend build/typecheck - frontend-only change, no backend touched). Deployed via `docker compose -f docker-compose.production.yml up -d --build nginx --no-deps` (frontend-only, backend left untouched deliberately per the `--build nginx bounces backend` gotcha). Fixed properly by having `gatherInputs` return the enrollment id it had already loaded, rather than the writer re-querying. This is the second time today `as any` hid something real. **The unchanged-record rule mirrors a lesson the artifact sync learned in production:** `compileAndStore` byte-compares the serialised record against what is stored and returns `unchanged` rather than inserting a duplicate version. Determinism buys nothing unless something persists the result and compares against it — there, the missing comparison meant a fresh commit on every upload forever; here it would mean a version history that grows on every page view and buries the versions representing real work. **Compiling never publishes.** It writes `content_json` and leaves `status`/`visibility` as found, so a record stays current for its owner without becoming a link; sharing is a separate deliberate act gated on `isShareable`. **Why `repo_path`/`commit_sha` are written on EVERY successful pass, not only when a commit happened:** an `unchanged` result still means the file is present at that path, and a row whose path was never stored would otherwise stay unlinkable forever purely because it synced before this existed — so the one student already syncing gets their paths recorded on the next run with no migration. Fail-soft per row: bookkeeping must never turn a successful sync into an error the student sees. **Three of five bands now compile** (identity, system, artifacts). Competencies and community posts resolve to `[]` because their readers are not written — deliberately absent rather than faked, and `recordGaps` correctly withholds sharing. **Still to build:** those two readers, and the page at `/p/<slug>`.

  - Notes: **Two real defects caught in my own code during the BREAK pass, before either shipped.** First, `mapSharedPosts` picked one post per week by timestamp, but `findAll` carried no `ORDER BY` — two posts sharing a timestamp resolved by whatever order Postgres produced, so the record would version on every compile while nothing had changed. That is the same class of bug as a clock in a pure compiler: non-determinism upstream defeats determinism downstream. Fixed with an explicit `ORDER BY` at the query AND an id tiebreak in the pure function, so it is correct on its own rather than correct only when well fed. Second, an absent or unparseable `updated_at` produced `NaN`, and every `NaN` comparison is false, which silently kept whichever row arrived first; it now sorts as 0 and loses to any real timestamp. Both have tests asserting order-independence in both directions. **One defect documented rather than fixed, deliberately.** A published record is served from the stored snapshot, which is what keeps an already-sent link stable — but that means clearing `shared_to_portfolio` changes what the reader returns without touching a snapshot compiled while the flag was set, so the post stays on the live public page until something recompiles. No student can grant consent yet (there is no UI), so this is latent rather than live, which is exactly why the requirement is written at the top of `capstoneReaders.ts` where whoever builds the toggle will read it: the toggle MUST call `compileAndStore` in the same request, and "I unshared it" has to mean the page changed, not that a column changed. **Why the nginx header rather than the React meta tag:** this is a SPA, so a crawler that does not execute JavaScript never sees a tag injected at runtime. The page injects one as best effort; the header is what actually holds. It is blanket-noindex across `/p/` because nginx cannot know a record's visibility without asking the API — erring toward not-indexed is the safe direction, since the reverse is unrecoverable once a crawler has the page. **Consent defaults off and is per post** because week 1's Roll Call is often candid about frustration at a named current employer, and republishing that under the student's real name beside their real repo would be a harm the platform caused, not the student. **State after this:** competencies render for 28 students immediately; the posts band stays empty until a consent UI exists; no record carries a headline yet because `deriveHeadline` reads the week-12 manifesto and no cohort has reached week 12. ### The /p/ noindex header was in the config, in the container, and not in the response (2026-08-24)
- [x] **Fixed a header I shipped hours earlier that never actually applied. `try_files`' SPA fallback internally redirects into `location = /index.html`, whose own `add_header` directives make nginx discard every inherited one — including the `X-Robots-Tag` that keeps unlisted student portfolios out of search.**
  - Date: 2026-08-24
  - Session: CC-20260819-i8it
  - What changed: **`nginx/nginx.conf` + `nginx/nginx.dev.conf`** — the `location ^~ /p/` block now ends in `rewrite ^ /index.html break;` instead of `try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;`, and sets `Pragma`/`Expires` alongside `Cache-Control` so the shell's cache behaviour matches every other SPA route. `break` stops rewrite processing and serves the file from THIS location, so the location's `add_header` directives survive; nothing real is served from under `/p/` (all assets come from `/static/`), so rewriting the whole prefix to the shell costs nothing.

### The unchanged-check that never fired once: JSONB does not preserve key order (2026-08-24)
- [x] **`compileAndStore` compared the stored record to the freshly compiled one with `JSON.stringify`, which compares key ORDER. `content_json` is JSONB and Postgres rewrites key order on write, so the comparison was false every single time and every compile appended a version — the exact outcome the check was written to prevent.**
  - Date: 2026-08-24
  - Session: CC-20260819-i8it
  - What changed: **`services/capstone/capstoneRecordStore.ts`** — new exported `canonicalJson()` serialises with object keys sorted RECURSIVELY, and the unchanged-check now compares `canonicalJson(existing.content_json) === canonicalJson(compiled)` instead of raw `JSON.stringify`. Arrays are deliberately NOT reordered: JSONB preserves array order, and the record's arrays are meaningful sequences (artifacts in week order, posts in week order), so sorting them would hide a genuine reordering as "unchanged". **`__tests__/canonicalJson.test.ts` (new, 8 tests)** — the first reproduces the real production key orders on both sides and asserts that raw `JSON.stringify` disagrees while `canonicalJson` matches, so the bug cannot come back silently.
  - Verification: **Found by running the real thing in production, not by reading code.** Compiled a record for a live project (Quincy Nkwain Ninying / CoreOps, `48f67531`): 18 competencies, 11 artifacts, all 11 carrying a repo path and commit SHA. Ran it a second time with nothing changed in between; it returned `outcome: "updated"`, `version: 2`. Proved the contents were identical by comparing the two stored versions' md5 inside Postgres — `24ece92f3400e66ec1f28900b607f9dd` for both — so the divergence was purely JS-side. Confirmed the mechanism directly in the backend container: stored key order `posts,system,bookend,identity,artifacts,competencies,schema_version` vs compiled `schema_version,identity,system,artifacts,competencies,posts,bookend`, `JSON.stringify` equal = false, canonical equal = true. After the fix: **Jest 86 passed across five capstone suites** (up from 78), backend `tsc --noEmit` exit 0.
  - Notes: **This is the third defect of the day found by exercising the running system rather than the artifact that produced it, and the pattern is now unmistakable.** The boot wiring was defined and never called. The nginx header was in the config, in the container, and not in the response. This comparison was correct as written and wrong against the storage engine underneath it. In every case the code read correctly and the tests passed; only the live system disagreed. **Why unit tests could not have caught this one:** the compiler's determinism is tested from literals, and both sides of the comparison were built in JS, where key order is insertion order and the check passes. The failure only exists after a round trip through JSONB, which no unit test performed. The new test encodes the round-tripped key order as a literal so the coverage no longer depends on having a database. **Byte-comparing a value that has been through JSONB is a trap worth naming generally:** JSONB is not a text format, it is a parsed representation, and Postgres normalises key order (by key length, then bytewise) and drops duplicate keys. Anything comparing `JSON.stringify` of a JSONB read against a freshly built object has this bug, whether or not it has noticed. **Also verified end-to-end on the real public domain during this work:** the app is at `enterprise.colaberry.ai` (not `colaberry.ai`, which is a separate Next.js property); `/p/anything` returns 200 with `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow` surviving Cloudflare, `/leaderboard` carries no robots header, and `/api/public/capstone/<unknown>` 404s.

Probable cause: the platform sends that one event via `navigator.sendBeacon(url, jsonString)`, which sets `Content-Type: text/plain`, so `express.json()` never parses the body; `scroll` travels the ordinary `fetch` path, which is exactly why scroll has `event_data` and `time_on_page` does not. v2 sidesteps it by construction - its `send()` already uses `fetch(..., keepalive: true)` with an explicit JSON content type, which is what `sendBeacon` was reaching for. **The platform fix is deliberately NOT in this change**: it touches every page of the main site and deserves its own PR and its own verification, not a rider on a brand-SDK change. Phases 4 and 5 remain: portal instrumentation plus `jx` in cross-brand links, then the cross-brand admin view.

Every item the parser will discard is now reported as an exclusion. **It refuses to hand over an empty project** - zero requirements looks identical to a silent failure, and the customer would be paying for a build with nothing in it. Proposals cross only when accepted and are labelled `(proposed)` in the document.

A voice agent that pushes past a brush-off is harassment, and these are the people least able to afford it.

## What is NOT done: activating CPN voice

The script and the safety fix are in. **No call can be placed for CPN yet, and that is deliberate** - three things remain, one of which cannot ship in code:

1. `scholarship_interview_call` entry point, seeded, with phone required.
2. The voice option on `/scholarships/`, beside the written interview as an equal path with explicit consent.
3. **A `RoutingRule` row mapping (source `cpn`, entry `scholarship_interview_call`) to the `request_callback` action.** Routing rules are not seeded in code - they are created through the admin API - so this is a production step a deploy cannot carry. It is the fourth instance this session of data that does not ship itself.

Until (3) exists nothing routes CPN to voice, so this change is inert for CPN and purely protective for everyone else.

The voice door now sits on `/scholarships/` beside the written interview at equal weight, with consent that names the AI, the recording and the call. `scholarship_interview_call` is seeded with phone AND email required, because `request_callback` refuses without either and an optional phone would produce a form that submits happily and never rings. New `seedRoutingRules.ts` makes the rule shippable rather than an admin-API step.
  - Verification: 36 tests across 4 suites; `tsc --noEmit` 0 errors, 0 error lines, unpiped; site harness green across 8 routes x 4 viewports; boundary validator OK, 16 files.

A scholarship applicant would have been answered by the bootcamp's callback line: a person asking a charity for help, spoken to as a sales lead, in a voice that is not ours. CPN now has its own slot with NO fallback, so unset means silence rather than substitution, and a test pins that it skips with `no_agent_id` instead of borrowing. **One manual step removed, one that cannot be.** Routing rules were admin-API-only, so `seedRoutingRules.ts` now ships the CPN rule - narrow by design: seeded by name, never deletes or deactivates, and operator-tuned rules including AI Flotation's are untouched, because a seeder asserting the full set would silently undo somebody's 3am tuning. What remains external is `SYNTHFLOW_CPN_AGENT_ID`: somebody must create a shell agent in the Synthflow dashboard and set it on prod. Until then every CPN call skips with `no_agent_id` and none is placed. **The voice door is beside the written interview, not beneath it** - the decision was that voice is an equal path, so it is not a smaller, greyer box under the real one.

## Deploy sequence for this change

1. backend rebuild (prompt selection, agent slot, seeds)
2. nginx rebuild (`/scholarships/` voice door)
3. `node dist/seeds/seedLeadSources.js` - the `scholarship_interview_call` entry point
4. `node dist/seeds/seedRoutingRules.js` - the rule that fires the call
5. **External, and not ours:** create the Synthflow shell agent, set `SYNTHFLOW_CPN_AGENT_ID`, restart backend

Steps 1-4 are safe without 5: the form accepts, the lead is captured and attributed, and the call skips with a visible reason rather than dialling in the wrong voice.
